META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 3.2 (8 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: General Science
UNIT.content:
• Terms used in linear motion (distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration)
• Equations of linear motion with constant acceleration (no derivations needed)
• Examples of linear motion with constant acceleration
• Freely falling bodies and the effect of gravity
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Communication and Collaboration: as the learner works with peers to discuss and present in plenary the application of linear motion in real life.
• Learning to Learn: as the learner carries out assignments on examples of bodies under free-fall motion and presents the findings in a group discussion.
UNIT.values:
• Peace: the learner displays tolerance and calmness when discussing the application of linear motion in real life.
• Unity: the learner displays cooperation and collaboration with others while investigating the effect of gravity on objects.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions and Defining Problems: as the learner formulates questions about why dropped objects speed up and how gravity influences free fall near Nairobi and other locations.
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: as the learner drops objects from measured heights to observe increasing speed and infer the effect of gravity.
• Analysing and Interpreting Data: as the learner uses collected timing data from free-fall observations to calculate acceleration due to gravity and compare with g = 10 m/s².
• Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking: as the learner solves numerical problems on linear motion using the equations of motion with constant acceleration.
• Constructing Explanations: as the learner explains observed differences in the speed of objects dropped from different heights using the concept of gravitational acceleration.
• Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information: as the learner researches applications of linear motion and free fall using digital and print media and presents findings to peers.
UNIT.pcis:
• Road Safety: increased awareness on how to minimise fatal injuries resulting from road crashes on sloping roads using the concept of free fall of objects (e.g., lorries descending the steep Kinangop escarpment or the Limuru–Nairobi road).
• Life Skills Education (Self-Awareness): the learner observes safety measures when dropping objects to investigate the effect of gravity on objects.
UNIT.careers:
• Civil and Structural Engineering: understanding linear motion and free fall is essential for designing safe roads, bridges, and buildings in Kenya's expanding infrastructure (e.g., the Nairobi Expressway, SGR).
• Sports Science and Athletics: Kenyan elite runners and jumpers (e.g., athletes from the Rift Valley) rely on principles of velocity, acceleration, and displacement for performance analysis and coaching.
• Aviation and Aerospace Technology: free-fall calculations and motion equations underpin pilot training and the growing Aviation track at Senior School.
• Traffic and Road Safety Management: NTSA officers and road engineers apply motion equations to set speed limits and design warning systems on steep Kenyan roads.
• Medicine and Biomechanics: understanding free fall and impact forces informs injury prevention and rehabilitation for falls — relevant to Kenya's hospitals and physiotherapy sector.
UNIT.focus: This unit develops learners' ability to describe, quantify, and apply the principles of linear motion — from defining key terms to solving real-world problems using the equations of constant acceleration and investigating free fall. Instruction anchors physics concepts in Kenyan everyday contexts such as road safety on escarpment roads, the flight path of a maize cob dropped from a granary, and the sprint mechanics of Rift Valley athletes. Learners progress from qualitative understanding of motion vocabulary to quantitative problem-solving and experimental investigation of gravitational acceleration.
UNIT.phenomenon: A mkokoteni (hand-cart) loaded with sacks of maize is accidentally released from rest at the top of the steep Limuru–Nairobi escarpment road and rolls freely downhill. Witnesses describe how it starts moving slowly but becomes dangerously fast within seconds, eventually crashing. Students view a short video clip of a runaway vehicle on a Kenyan escarpment road and are asked: "Why does the cart keep getting faster even though no one is pushing it, and could we have predicted how fast it would be going before it crashed?" This is puzzling because the cart has no engine, yet its speed continuously increases — suggesting an invisible force (gravity) is continuously doing work on it. The phenomenon directly motivates the need to define motion terms precisely, develop equations that can predict the cart's speed and distance at any moment, and understand free fall as the purest expression of gravitational acceleration.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A ripe mango falling from a tree on a Kisumu farm — students notice it falls faster and faster rather than at a constant speed, raising the question of what determines how quickly it accelerates.
• A Kenyan 100 m sprinter (e.g., a school athletics champion) filmed from the starting blocks — the video shows the athlete accelerating from rest to top speed, illustrating real-world non-uniform linear motion with measurable displacement and time intervals.
• A water tank filling on a Nairobi rooftop where a pipe drips at constant intervals — drops photographed with a phone stroboscope show increasing spacing between successive positions, providing visual evidence of acceleration under gravity.
• A matatu braking to a stop on Mombasa Road — passengers lurch forward, prompting discussion of deceleration (negative acceleration), braking distance, and road safety.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: Why does a runaway mkokoteni on the Limuru escarpment keep getting faster — and how can we use mathematics to predict exactly how fast and how far it will travel before it crashes?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How is free fall motion important in real life?
2. How can the dangers of free fall in our day-to-day life be mitigated?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1 — Anchoring Phenomenon & Motion Vocabulary: Students watch a video clip of a runaway vehicle on a steep Kenyan escarpment road. They record initial observations and predictions about why the vehicle accelerates. The teacher facilitates a whole-class discussion to surface prior knowledge and misconceptions. Students are introduced to and distinguish between distance, displacement, speed, velocity, and acceleration using the mkokoteni scenario and Kenyan athletics examples. A class Driving Question Board (DQB) is created and initial questions are posted.

Lesson 2 — Equations of Linear Motion (Part 1): Using the mkokoteni context, the teacher introduces the four equations of linear motion with constant acceleration (presented without derivation as per KICD). Students identify the five variables (u, v, a, s, t) and practise selecting the correct equation for given problems. Worked examples use Kenyan road and athletics contexts (e.g., a matatu accelerating from a bus stop on Thika Road). Students solve structured numerical problems in pairs.

Lesson 3 — Equations of Linear Motion (Part 2 — Problem Solving): Students work in small groups to solve a set of progressively challenging problems using all four equations of motion, including contexts such as a Rift Valley athlete's 400 m race, a boda-boda decelerating before a police check, and a ball thrown upward from a Mombasa rooftop. Groups present solutions on the board; the teacher uses cold-calling (minimum 3 groups per problem set) and provides 30-second wait time before taking responses. The DQB is updated with new insights.

Lesson 4 — Investigating Free Fall (Predict & Observe): Students first predict: "If you drop a ripe mango and a pebble from the same height, which hits the ground first?" They record predictions individually. The class then drops objects (rubber bung, crumpled paper, stone) from a fixed height of 2 m and observes that all reach the ground at the same time (in the absence of significant air resistance). Students infer that gravity accelerates all objects equally. Data on drop height and time are recorded and used to estimate g.

Lesson 5 — Freely Falling Bodies (Explain & Calculate): Students use their experimental data from Lesson 4 and the equations of linear motion (with u = 0, a = g ≈ 10 m/s²) to calculate the speed of the mkokoteni at various points along the escarpment, the time taken for the mango to fall from the tree, and the height from which an object was dropped given its impact speed. The teacher explicitly connects each calculation back to the anchoring phenomenon. Students discuss the dangers of free fall on sloping surfaces and steep roads in Kenya.

Lesson 6 — Applications, Road Safety & Real-Life Contexts: Using the equations and free-fall principles, students investigate the braking distance of a matatu travelling at different speeds on Mombasa Road. They discuss road safety (NTSA guidelines, signage on steep roads such as the Kinangop descent) and how understanding linear motion can save lives. Students research (using digital devices or print media) one additional real-life application of linear motion in Kenya (e.g., SGR train scheduling, pole-vault athletics, construction safety) and prepare a brief group presentation.

Lesson 7 — Group Presentations & Model Building: Groups present their real-life application research from Lesson 6 (3 minutes per group; teacher cold-calls 2 members per group for follow-up questions). The class collaboratively builds and refines a visual explanatory model (annotated diagram or motion-time graph sequence) connecting the anchoring phenomenon — the mkokoteni on the escarpment — to all sub-strand concepts: motion terms, equations, free fall, gravity, and road safety mitigation. The DQB is reviewed and students identify which questions have been answered and which remain.

Lesson 8 — Consolidation, DQB Review & Assessment: Students individually solve a structured set of problems revisiting all four equations and free fall, set in the context of the anchoring phenomenon (the mkokoteni) and supporting phenomena (Kenyan sprinter, falling mango). The class conducts a final DQB review — remaining questions are discussed and answered collectively. Students reflect in their journals on how their thinking about the anchoring phenomenon has changed since Lesson 1, articulating the role of gravity, constant acceleration, and the equations of motion in explaining and predicting the mkokoteni's dangerous descent.

LESSONS.title: The Runaway Mkokoteni: Why Does It Keep Getting Faster?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: mkokoteni, Limuru escarpment, distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration, gravity, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon of the runaway mkokoteni, to give learners precise definitions of distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration, and to establish the claim that the cart's velocity keeps increasing (it accelerates), while opening the Driving Question Board.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to explain terms used in linear motion (distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration): distance is total path length (scalar, m); displacement is straight-line change in position with direction (vector, m); speed is distance/time (scalar); velocity is displacement/time (vector); acceleration is change in velocity per unit time (m/s²). Learners also state that the cart's speed rises by 2 m/s every second, so it accelerates.
slo.skills: Observing and recording data from a video; making and justifying predictions; asking scientific questions; distinguishing scalar from vector quantities using a 400 m lap; developing an initial model (annotated sketch) of the cart's motion; communicating ideas in whole-class discussion.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the significance of linear motion in real life and road safety; respect others' opinions during discussion (Respect); show tolerance and calmness when ideas differ (Peace); cooperate with peers in groups (Unity). Core competencies: Communication and collaboration; Learning to learn. PCI: Road safety.
slo.keyInquiry: How is free fall motion important in real life? How can the dangers of free fall in our day-to-day life be mitigated? (Lesson driving question: Why does a runaway mkokoteni on the Limuru escarpment keep getting faster, and how can we use mathematics to predict exactly how fast and how far it will travel before it crashes?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the launch lesson. It introduces the phenomenon of Mzee Kamau's runaway mkokoteni (300 kg loaded, released from rest on the Limuru-Nairobi escarpment, crashing into a parked lorry after 100 m in 10 s). It surfaces prior ideas, gives the vocabulary needed for all later lessons, and creates the DQB. Lesson 2 will build on the definitions of velocity and acceleration to develop equations that let learners predict the cart's speed and distance.
slo.safetyNotes: Use a 400 m track or marked school field only in a controlled way for the walking and running demonstration; keep the learners walking, not racing. Keep the area clear of vehicles and obstacles. In the discussion, treat the road crash sensitively: nobody was hurt in the incident, only the cart was destroyed, and some learners may have experienced road accidents. Do not let learners test anything on real slopes or with real carts.

LESSONS.overview: Learners meet the phenomenon: Mzee Kamau, a vegetable and maize seller, was helping a customer when his loaded mkokoteni (cart 50 kg + 5 sacks of maize at 50 kg each = 300 kg) rolled away from rest down a steep straight section of the Limuru-Nairobi escarpment road. The bystander Achieng says, 'It started slowly then flew.' It crashed into a parked lorry after 100 m, about 10 s later. Learners predict why it speeds up with no engine and no one pushing, watch a short video of a runaway vehicle on a Kenyan escarpment road, and record observations. They then use the cart and Kenyan athletics (a 400 m lap) to distinguish distance from displacement and speed from velocity, and are introduced to acceleration as the rate at which velocity changes. The class uses the average speed of 10 m/s (100 m in 10 s) and the idea that the cart's speed rises by 2 m/s every second, without any equations yet. The lesson ends with the class building the Driving Question Board and a first annotated sketch model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually read the story of Mzee Kamau's mkokoteni and Achieng's remark, 'It started slowly then flew.' In their science notebooks they sketch a graph of speed against time that they think matches the cart (no formulas needed), and write 2 to 3 sentences answering: 'Why does the cart keep getting faster even though no one is pushing it, and could we have predicted how fast it would be going before it crashed?' They also write one number guess: how fast (km/h) was it going when it hit the lorry? They share with a partner for 2 minutes and then record a class poll of guesses on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Read the story aloud slowly. Say: 'Mzee Kamau turns away for a moment. The cart has no engine. Nobody is pushing. What do you think happens next?' Give individual silent WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after the main question before anyone speaks, then 4 minutes of writing. Circulate and photograph or note 3 contrasting predictions (for example 'it speeds up because of gravity', 'the maize weight pushes it', 'it keeps one steady speed'). Cold-call 4 learners, including at least 2 who have not volunteered, with: 'Tell us your prediction and one reason.' Do not say which is correct. Record each prediction on the board under the heading 'Our first ideas'. Say: 'Hold on to these. We will check them against evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-then-test with a claim and reason (Asking Questions and Defining Problems; Developing and Using Models): committing to a written prediction and a sketch graph before instruction makes prior ideas visible, so that learners can later see how their thinking changed, and gives the teacher data on misconceptions such as 'a moving object needs a continuing push' or 'heavier objects speed up more'.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) each learner has written a prediction with a reason; (2) the sketched graph is either flat (constant speed), rising, or something else, which diagnoses whether the learner expects speeding up; (3) the number guess in km/h shows their sense of scale. Tally on a quick checklist how many predicted 'speeds up', 'steady speed', or 'speeds up because heavy'. Note any learner who refers to gravity, and any who says the cart needs a push to keep moving. Do not grade; use only to plan the discussion.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners watch a short video clip (about 2 minutes, played twice) of a runaway vehicle on a steep Kenyan escarpment road (for example a clip shared by the teacher from a news report; if no video is available, the teacher uses a prepared picture strip of the cart at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 s positions, with the spacing between pictures increasing). In groups of four they complete an observation table with three columns: 'What I saw', 'What I noticed about the speed at the start, middle and end', and 'What I wonder'. They then record, as a class, the facts of the case: starting from rest, slope steep and straight, no engine, no one pushing, crash after 100 m in about 10 s. The teacher shows the average speed: 100 m in 10 s gives 10 m/s on average, and reveals that the cart was moving at about 72 km/h at the end, so it must have been much slower at the start. Learners compare the picture spacing to see that the distance covered in each second keeps growing.
framework.teacherMoves: Before playing say: 'Watch the first two seconds and the last two seconds. Do not write during the first viewing; just watch the speed.' Play once with no pause, then say: 'Turn to your group and say in one sentence what you noticed about the speed.' After the second viewing give 3 minutes to fill in the table. Circulate with the question: 'How do you know it is going faster, and what are you comparing?' Press with: 'Is it covering more distance each second, or the same?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'What is the evidence that speed is changing?' Cold-call 3 groups to share one observation each, and write them on the board under 'Evidence'. Reveal the facts: 100 m, about 10 s, average speed 10 m/s. Ask: 'If the average is 10 m/s and it ended at 20 m/s, what does that tell us about the start?' Wait 10-15 seconds. Let learners reason that it started at 0 and rose steadily. Say: 'Its speed went up by about 2 m/s every single second.' Do not give the equations; say only that Lesson 2 will show how to predict this.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured observation with data comparison (Analyzing and Interpreting Data): learners separate what they saw from what they infer, and using picture spacing and average speed they find the pattern that speed keeps increasing. The pattern becomes the phenomenon-level claim that the cart is accelerating.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the observation tables for: (1) at least one observation stating that speed changes (for example 'slow at first, fast at the end'); (2) separation of observation from explanation; (3) correct use of the facts that average speed is 100 m / 10 s = 10 m/s. Listen for groups that notice growing gaps between positions. Ask exit-ticket style thumbs: 'Thumbs up if you think the cart went at the same speed throughout.' Count the hands. Reteach with the picture strip if more than a quarter agree.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners build the precise motion vocabulary in three steps. (1) The 400 m lap: the class goes outside (or imagines the track) with an athlete in the Rift Valley style 400 m race; a volunteer walks one full lap of a marked 400 m (or scaled) track. Learners decide the distance (400 m, total path) and displacement (0 m, because they end where they started) and discuss why the numbers differ. (2) Speed and velocity: learners compare 'speed is distance/time' with 'velocity is displacement/time, with direction', then use the cart: 'The cart moves 100 m down the slope in 10 s: its average speed is 10 m/s, and its velocity is 10 m/s down the slope.' They convert 72 km/h to 20 m/s by dividing by 3.6. (3) Acceleration: they use the statement that the cart's velocity rises by 2 m/s every second to define acceleration as change in velocity per unit time, in m/s², so the cart's acceleration is 2 m/s². They fill a Frayer-style vocabulary card for each of the five terms with definition, scalar or vector, unit, a cart example and a Kenyan athletics example. In pairs they classify a list of statements (for example 'Mzee Kamau's cart travelled 100 m', 'the cart moved 100 m down the slope', 'the cart's speed was 10 m/s on average', 'the cart's speed rose by 2 m/s each second') into the correct term. Finally, they write a one-sentence claim: 'The cart accelerates because its velocity increases steadily from zero.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A Kenyan 400 m runner finishes a full lap. How far did she run, and how far is she from where she started?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners (one from each side of the room). Write 'distance = 400 m' and 'displacement = 0 m' side by side and ask: 'Why can both be true?' Then ask: 'If she took 50 s, what is her average speed? And her average velocity?' Wait 10-15 seconds; guide to 8 m/s and 0 m/s. Draw the cart on the slope and say: 'Same question for the cart: it moved 100 m in a straight line down the slope. Is the distance equal to the displacement here? Why?' Then say: 'At the start the velocity is 0. After 1 s it is 2 m/s. After 2 s it is 4 m/s. What do you notice about how much it changes each second?' Wait 10-15 seconds; cold-call 2 learners. Introduce acceleration only as 'change in velocity each second', and write 'a = 2 m/s²' and what it means in words. Do not derive or use the equations of linear motion; say: 'Next lesson we will learn how to use this to predict the cart's speed at any moment.' Address misconceptions: 'Speed and acceleration are not the same: a fast cart can have zero acceleration, and a cart can have a small speed with large acceleration.' Use one question to probe: 'At the very first moment the velocity is zero. Is the acceleration also zero? Explain.' Cold-call 2 learners. Emphasise respect: 'Listen to each idea, then build on it.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Contrasting cases and Frayer vocabulary cards (Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking; Constructing Explanations): placing distance and displacement, and speed and velocity, side by side with the 400 m lap lets learners see exactly what changes between the two, and connecting each definition to the cart anchors the abstract terms to the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners correctly state the 400 m lap as distance 400 m and displacement 0 m; (2) the vocabulary cards give correct units (m, m/s, m/s²) and mark distance and speed as scalar, displacement, velocity and acceleration as vector; (3) in the classification task, at least 80% of statements are placed correctly; (4) the final claim mentions that velocity increases steadily. Use a quick whiteboard check: 'Show me the unit of acceleration.' Note learners who write m/s instead of m/s² and revisit with 'change in velocity (m/s) every second'.

framework.learnerExperience: The class builds the Driving Question Board on a wall chart headed with the driving question: 'Why does a runaway mkokoteni on the Limuru escarpment keep getting faster, and how can we use mathematics to predict exactly how fast and how far it will travel before it crashes?' Each learner writes 2 questions on sticky notes or strips about the phenomenon (for example 'Why does gravity make it faster?', 'Would a heavier cart go faster?', 'How fast would it be after 5 s?', 'What if it fell straight down?', 'How can drivers on steep roads like Kinangop stay safe?'). In groups of four they sort questions into categories (for example 'Why does it speed up?', 'How can we predict?', 'Free fall and gravity', 'Road safety'). Groups post their questions on the DQB and each group reads out one favourite. The two KICD inquiry questions are added: 'How is free fall motion important in real life?' and 'How can the dangers of free fall in our day-to-day life be mitigated?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You now know the facts of the case and some new words. What are you still wondering? Write questions that start with Why, How, What if.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Which questions can we only answer by measuring or calculating?' Model a good question: 'How could we calculate the speed after 5 s?' Show how to rewrite a weak question ('Is gravity strong?') into a stronger one ('How does gravity change the speed of the cart each second?'). Cold-call 4 groups to read one question each and ask the class: 'Which category does this belong to?' Point to the questions that need the equations of linear motion and tell learners these will be answered in Lessons 2 and 3. Link road safety questions to the PCI: 'The NTSA is concerned about runaway vehicles on steep roads, so your road safety questions are real questions.' Keep the board visible and say: 'We will return to this board in every lesson and move questions to the Answered column.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question sorting (Asking Questions and Defining Problems): learners generate and categorise their own questions, which gives purpose to the unit, makes the class's curiosity visible, and lets them see that mathematics is needed to answer 'how fast' and 'how far'.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) every learner posts at least two questions; (2) at least some questions are testable or calculable, not only yes/no; (3) categories chosen by groups are sensible and refer to the phenomenon; (4) learners can say which of their questions need measurement or calculation. Use a quick tally on the DQB categories to see which ideas (gravity, prediction, free fall, safety) the class cares about. Provide a sentence starter ('How could we find out...') to learners who struggle.

framework.learnerExperience: Individually, learners draw an initial model of the runaway mkokoteni on a half page of the notebook: an annotated diagram of the slope with the cart at five positions (0 s, 2 s, 4 s, 6 s, 10 s at increasing spacing), labels for the direction of motion, an arrow showing gravity pulling it down the slope, and a rough speed-time sketch that rises from zero. Using colour, they annotate where the velocity is small and where it is large and write a caption using at least three of the five terms: 'The cart accelerates at 2 m/s² because its velocity increases by 2 m/s every second.' In pairs they compare, add one improvement each, and write one thing the model cannot yet do (for example 'it cannot tell us the speed at 7 s'). The sketches are kept in a Model folder to be revised in later lessons. Finish with an exit ticket: 'Write one thing you used to think about the cart that you now think differently, and one question you still have.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A model is a drawing that explains and helps predict. Show the motion, the direction, and what is changing.' Display an example with only the slope and arrows as a starting point (not a complete answer). Circulate and ask: 'Which part of your drawing shows that the cart is accelerating?' and 'Where does the gravity arrow go, and why along the slope?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 learners to explain their models in 30 seconds; ask the class to give 'one star and one wish'. Highlight that the gaps between cart positions must increase. Close by saying: 'Our model is a first draft. In Lesson 2 we will learn the equations of linear motion so it can predict the cart's speed and position at any time.' Collect exit tickets. Check misconceptions: if a learner draws constant spacing, ask: 'What would that mean for the speed?' Ask learners to keep their predictions from the Predict Phase for comparison in Lesson 8.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial model construction and revision (Developing and Using Models): learners combine the diagram, gravity arrow, spacing and speed sketch into one representation of the phenomenon, which they can test and improve as new ideas arrive. Naming what the model cannot yet do shows the need for mathematics.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check for: (1) spacing between positions increases; (2) a gravity or downhill arrow is drawn along the slope; (3) the caption uses at least three of the terms distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration correctly; (4) the speed-time sketch starts at zero and rises; (5) the exit ticket shows a change in thinking. Mark each indicator as Yes/Partly/Not yet on a class list. Learners who draw equal spacing or a flat graph get a brief one-to-one conversation and the picture strip from the Observe Phase.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: (1) Did learners separate observation from explanation in the video task? (2) Which misconceptions appeared in the predictions (for example the cart needs a continuous push, heavier objects speed up more, speed and acceleration are the same), and how many learners held them? (3) Could learners explain why the 400 m lap has distance 400 m but displacement 0 m? (4) Did I give enough WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds and cold-call a range of learners, including quieter ones and learners from different groups? (5) Which DQB questions need Lessons 2-3, which need the free fall investigation, and which concern road safety? (6) What changes will I make to pacing, for example less time on the vocabulary cards and more on the model? Record the three most common prediction types to compare with learners' final explanations in Lesson 8.

The cart's velocity rises by 2 m/s every second, so it accelerates at 2 m/s².
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The cart has no engine and no one pushing it, yet it keeps getting faster because gravity pulls it down the slope all the time, so its velocity increases steadily from zero. LESSONS.title: Equations of Linear Motion: Choosing the Right Equation
LESSONS.aresKeywords: linear motion, constant acceleration, initial velocity, final velocity, displacement, time, equations of linear motion, matatu, mkokoteni, Limuru escarpment

slo.purpose: Learners use the four equations of linear motion to turn the cart's constant acceleration idea from Lesson 1 into numbers, so they can predict its speed and distance at any moment.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) identify the five variables of linear motion (u, v, a, s, t) with their SI units; (b) state the four equations of linear motion for constant acceleration, given without derivation: (1) v = u + at; (2) s = ut + ½at²; (3) v² = u² + 2as; (4) s = ½(u+v)t; (c) select the equation that links the three known variables and the one unknown; (d) check the equations against the first rows of the mkokoteni table (t = 1 to 5 s).
slo.skills: Analysing and interpreting data (NGSS SEP 4); using mathematics and computational thinking (SEP 5): listing knowns and unknown, selecting an equation, substituting with units, and checking that answers are reasonable; constructing explanations (SEP 6).
slo.attitudes: Perseverance and precision with units; respect for peers' reasoning (Respect); cooperation in pair work (Unity); willingness to check own answers before accepting them. Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving; Communication and collaboration. PCI: Road safety.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD Key Inquiry Question 1: How is free fall motion important in real life? (Lesson 2 builds the mathematical tools needed to answer it.) Driving question: Why does a runaway mkokoteni on the Limuru escarpment keep getting faster, and how can we use mathematics to predict exactly how fast and how far it will travel before it crashes?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 gave learners the vocabulary (distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration) and the claim that the cart's velocity keeps increasing. Lesson 2 supplies the prediction tools: the four equations and a method for choosing among them. Learners test the tools on a matatu on Thika Road, then check them against the first rows of the mkokoteni table (a = 2 m/s², t = 1 to 5 s). Lesson 3 will extend the method to multi-step problems, deceleration and upward motion. This lesson does not teach free fall, stopping distances or graphs.
slo.safetyNotes: Mostly a desk-based lesson. Keep bags and chairs out of walkways during pair work. If any learner walks a measured 10 m to estimate speed, use the corridor or field only with the teacher present. Calculators are optional; set shared-use rules.

LESSONS.overview: Learners start from the question 'Could we have predicted how fast the cart was going before it crashed?' and predict how speed and distance would grow each second. They then meet the matatu on Thika Road (u = 0, a = 1.5 m/s², t = 8 s), where the teacher models the method: list the five variables, mark knowns and the unknown, and pick the equation that contains exactly those four. The four equations are given without derivation, as the KICD design requires. Learners then use them to check the first rows of the mkokoteni table (t = 1 to 5 s) against a = 2 m/s², which shows that v increases by 2 m/s each second while s grows as t². In pairs they solve structured problems, justify their equation choice in words, and add questions to the Driving Question Board. The lesson ends with the first update to the class model: the cart's acceleration is constant, so equations can predict its motion.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners recall the phenomenon: Mzee Kamau's loaded mkokoteni (300 kg) released from rest at the top of the Limuru-Nairobi escarpment, rolling 100 m to a parked lorry. Achieng said 'it started slowly then flew'. Individually, in their notebooks, learners predict: (a) the cart's speed after 1 s, 2 s and 5 s, and (b) the distance covered after 5 s compared with after 10 s. Then they write one sentence: 'To predict this exactly, we would need to know ___.' In pairs they compare predictions and note where they disagree. Learners also recall from Lesson 1 that acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time, and that the cart's velocity keeps rising.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the phenomenon image and say: 'Achieng said it started slowly then flew. Today we ask: could Mzee Kamau's neighbours have predicted exactly how fast it would be going?' Ask learners to write predictions silently. WAIT TIME: 12 seconds of silence before pair talk. Say: 'Do not look at your neighbour yet. Write numbers, even if you guess.' Cold-call 4 pairs to share their prediction for speed after 5 s, and record all four on the board without judging. Ask: 'What would you need to know about the cart to be sure?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds. Cold-call 2 more learners. Record the variables they name (starting speed, time, how quickly speed changes, distance) in a list headed 'What we need to know'. Do not name the symbols yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Share-Compare, with a 'What we need to know' list. Writing numerical predictions first exposes learners' existing ideas (some expect speed to be steady, others expect it to double). The learner-generated list of needed quantities prepares them to see the five variables as meaningful rather than arbitrary symbols.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners write numbers with units (m/s, m) rather than words only. Tally how many predict speed rising by equal amounts each second (consistent with constant acceleration) versus doubling each second or staying steady. Listen for: 'speed keeps going up each second' (linked to acceleration from Lesson 1). Note learners who confuse speed with distance. Check the board list: did learners name starting speed, time and rate of change of speed?

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Part A - Naming the variables: Learners are given a one-page card for the matatu on Thika Road: 'A matatu leaves a stage on Thika Road from rest, accelerates steadily at 1.5 m/s² for 8 s.' The class builds a variable table: u (initial velocity, m/s), v (final velocity, m/s), a (acceleration, m/s²), s (displacement, m), t (time, s). Learners mark each variable as 'known' or 'unknown' for the matatu: u = 0, a = 1.5 m/s², t = 8 s known; v and s unknown. Part B - The four equations: The teacher presents the four equations of linear motion, written exactly: (1) v = u + at; (2) s = ut + ½at²; (3) v² = u² + 2as; (4) s = ½(u+v)t. A note states they apply when acceleration is constant and are given without derivation. Learners underline which variable is MISSING from each equation: (1) no s; (2) no v; (3) no t; (4) no a. Part C - Using the method: The teacher models the matatu: to find v, list u = 0, a = 1.5, t = 8, choose equation (1): v = 0 + 1.5 x 8 = 12 m/s (43.2 km/h). To find s, choose equation (2): s = 0 + ½ x 1.5 x 8² = 48 m. Check with equation (4): s = ½(0+12) x 8 = 48 m. Part D - Test on the cart: Pairs complete the first rows of the mkokoteni table using u = 0, a = 2 m/s²: t = 1 s: v = 2 m/s, s = 1 m; t = 2 s: v = 4, s = 4; t = 3 s: v = 6, s = 9; t = 4 s: v = 8, s = 16; t = 5 s: v = 10, s = 25. They check that v rises by 2 m/s each second and that s grows as t² (1, 4, 9, 16, 25).
framework.teacherMoves: Hand out the Thika Road card. Say: 'Before choosing any equation, we list. Which of the five variables do we know? Which one are we hunting?' Cold-call 3 learners to name one variable each with its unit. WAIT TIME: 10 seconds after each question. Present the four equations on a prepared chart and say: 'These work only when acceleration is constant. We use them without deriving them, as the syllabus asks.' Ask: 'Which variable is missing from equation 3? Why might that help us?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds, then cold-call 2 learners. Model the matatu on the board while thinking aloud: 'I know u, a, t. I want v. Equation 1 has exactly these four. So I use it.' Write units at every step. Then ask: 'Is 12 m/s reasonable for a matatu after 8 s? Convert: 12 x 3.6 = 43.2 km/h.' Circulate during Part D. Say: 'Fill in v first with equation 1, then s with equation 2, and tell your partner which equation you used each time.' Pause the class at t = 3 s and ask 3 cold-called learners: 'What do you notice about the v column? And the s column?' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. Do NOT introduce t = 6, 8 or 10 s rows yet; learners may extend them as a challenge. Remind: 'The cart's acceleration is 2 m/s², not 10. The slope only provides a fraction of g. We will explore why in a later lesson.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Worked example with think-aloud, then 'List-Choose-Substitute-Check'. Modelling the thinking, not just the algebra, shows how an expert chooses an equation by matching knowns and unknown, which is the lesson's central skill. Testing the equations on the cart table lets learners see that the equations reproduce a pattern they could describe only in words in Lesson 1: velocity rising by 2 m/s each second.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that learners (a) list knowns and unknown BEFORE choosing an equation; (b) write units at each step; (c) state the missing-variable test for the equation they chose. Look for common errors: using v instead of u in equation 2; forgetting to square t; dividing by 3.6 in the wrong direction; using a = 10 for the cart. Observable success: pairs correctly complete five table rows (t = 1 to 5 s) with v = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 m/s and s = 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 m. Collect the Thika Road calculation as a quick exit check for 5 randomly selected learners.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Part A - Structured pair problems (Kenyan contexts): Pairs solve three problems, each requiring the learner to write a four-line solution (Knowns, Unknown, Equation chosen and why, Answer with units). Problem 1: A matatu on Thika Road accelerates from rest at 1.5 m/s² for 8 s; find the final velocity (12 m/s) and the displacement (48 m). Problem 2: Mzee Kamau's cart, from rest at a = 2 m/s², has covered s = 25 m; find the velocity at that point using equation (3) and no time: v² = 2 x 2 x 25 = 100, so v = 10 m/s. Learners confirm that this equals the table value at t = 5 s. Problem 3: A learner on a Kenyan school field jogs from rest and reaches 4 m/s in 2 s; find the acceleration (2 m/s²) and the distance covered (4 m), choosing from equations (1) and (4) or (2). Part B - Explain in words: Each pair writes 2 to 3 sentences answering: 'Why did the equation you chose work better than the others?' and 'Which variable did your chosen equation not need?' Part C - Link to the cart: Learners use the table to explain why the cart 'felt sudden': at t = 5 s, v = 10 m/s and s = 25 m, but the distance covered doubles twice over by t = 10 s (s = 100 m), because s grows as t². They write one sentence connecting this to Achieng's 'started slowly then flew'.
framework.teacherMoves: Pair learners by mixed confidence. Say: 'Partner A writes the knowns and unknown. Partner B chooses the equation and explains why. Then swap for the next problem.' Circulate with a checklist. Ask pairs: 'Which variable is missing from the equation you chose? How do you know that is the right one?' For pairs finishing early, pose: 'Can you solve Problem 1 using a different equation to check your answer?' After 12 minutes, stop the class: 'Pencils down. Turn to your partner and compare answers.' Cold-call 4 pairs to give the answer to Problem 1 and 3 pairs for Problem 2. WAIT TIME: 10 to 15 seconds before each cold call. For a wrong answer say: 'Interesting. Show us your knowns list.' and let the class locate the error rather than telling them. Facilitate a whole-class discussion: 'Why does the distance in the cart table grow so much faster than the speed?' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Close by asking: 'What did the equations let us do that Lesson 1's words could not?' Elicit: predict exact values.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning in pairs: the claim is the numerical answer, the evidence is the list of knowns and the substituted equation, and the reasoning is the written justification for the equation choice. Partner roles (writer and chooser, then swap) ensure that both learners practise the selection decision. Linking back to Achieng's statement turns numerical skill into an explanation of the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) 'Knowns and unknown' list present before any equation in at least 80 percent of written solutions; (b) correct equation chosen in Problems 1 to 3 (Problem 2 should use equation 3 because t is not given); (c) correct final values with units: 12 m/s, 48 m, 10 m/s, 2 m/s², 4 m; (d) written justification that names the missing variable. Use a 3-level tally: independent, with prompting, needs reteach. Plan a short reteach in Lesson 3 for learners who mix up u and v, or ignore the units.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) The DQB from Lesson 1 is displayed. Learners first review the questions already posted. Individually they write on sticky notes: (a) one question that Lesson 2 has ANSWERED or partly answered (for example, 'Can we predict the cart's speed at 5 s?' now answered: 10 m/s) and (b) one NEW question that the lesson raised (for example, 'What if the cart did not start from rest?', 'What if the matatu slows down instead?', 'Why is the cart's acceleration only 2 m/s² and not 10?', 'How are these equations used when an object falls straight down?'). They place notes on the DQB under the headings 'Answered/Partly answered' and 'New questions'. The class groups new questions by theme: slowing down, falling objects, the slope.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board from Lesson 1. Which questions did today's equations help with?' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to move a note to 'Answered' and say why. Say: 'Now write a question that today made you curious.' Collect notes and cluster them aloud. Highlight themes that connect to later lessons without teaching them: 'Questions about slowing down and objects thrown upward will come in Lesson 3. Questions about falling will come in Lessons 4 and 5. Why only 2 m/s² for the cart is a question we will return to.' Cold-call 2 learners to read a new question aloud.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: sorting questions into 'answered' and 'new' makes learning visible and shows learners that science progresses by answering questions and raising better ones. Clustering questions by theme shows how each upcoming lesson connects to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look at whether notes distinguish what was answered (for example 'speed at 5 s is 10 m/s') from what remains open. Quality of new questions: do they extend the equations to new conditions (deceleration, falling, non-zero start)? Note learners who write only vague questions ('What is acceleration?') and prompt them to refer to numbers. Check that at least 5 questions connect to free fall or the effect of the slope.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners begin the class model of the cart in their notebooks. Model v1 (from Lesson 1): a labelled diagram of the cart on the slope with the note 'velocity keeps increasing'. Learners now add: (a) the five variables labelled for the cart: u = 0 m/s, a = 2 m/s², and the table values for t = 1 to 5 s; (b) a short box titled 'Prediction tool' that lists the four equations of linear motion, and a one-line rule 'List knowns and unknown, then choose the equation that has those four variables'; (c) one sentence: 'Because acceleration is constant, we can predict v and s at any moment.' They also write in a 'Still to explain' box: 'Why is a only 2 m/s²?' and 'What if the cart slowed down or went up?' Learners complete the summary table (observed, learned, explained) for homework.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Lesson 1 model. We are not starting again. We are adding a prediction tool.' Model the first addition on the board: write u = 0 and a = 2 m/s² on the cart diagram. Ask learners to complete the rest independently. WAIT TIME: 10 seconds, then circulate. Cold-call 3 learners to read their one-sentence statement about constant acceleration and prediction. Ask: 'Which part of today's evidence supports your sentence?' Elicit: 'The table: velocity rose by 2 m/s every second, and s equalled t².' Remind learners that the equations apply when acceleration is constant, and that the cart on the slope has a = 2 m/s², not 10. Assign homework: complete the summary table and solve one extra problem: a matatu on Thika Road from rest at a = 1.5 m/s² travelling s = 48 m, find v using equation (3) (answer 12 m/s).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision (annotated diagram plus a prediction tool). Adding quantitative tools to the qualitative Lesson 1 model shows how mathematical reasoning strengthens an explanation. The 'Still to explain' box makes gaps visible, which motivates Lessons 3 to 5.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each model includes: (a) u = 0 and a = 2 m/s² labelled on the diagram; (b) at least two correct table values (for example v = 10 m/s and s = 25 m at t = 5 s); (c) the four equations written correctly; (d) a sentence linking constant acceleration to predictability. Watch for the misconception that a = 10 m/s² for the cart, or that the equations apply to any motion. Use a 3-point check (labelled diagram, equations, sentence) as a quick tally.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did learners list knowns and unknown BEFORE reaching for an equation, or did they hunt for numbers to plug in? (2) Which pairs could justify their choice using the missing-variable idea, and which just copied? (3) How many learners wrote a = 10 for the cart or mixed up u and v? (4) Were the table values for t = 1 to 5 s (v = 2 to 10 m/s, s = 1 to 25 m) enough for learners to see v rising by 2 m/s each second and s growing as t²? (5) Did the DQB notes show curiosity about slowing down and falling? Use these answers to plan a brief reteach at the start of Lesson 3, which builds on this lesson's selection method with the sign convention, negative acceleration and upward motion.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe or work out today? (Examples: the matatu on Thika Road reaches v = 12 m/s and s = 48 m after 8 s; the mkokoteni table for t = 1 to 5 s gives v = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 m/s and s = 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 m.)
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we learn about the equations of linear motion? (Include the five variables u, v, a, s, t with units, the four equations, and the rule for choosing: list the knowns and the unknown, then pick the equation that has exactly those four variables.)
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How does this help explain the driving question? (Use the cart's constant acceleration of 2 m/s² to explain why the velocity rises by 2 m/s every second, why the cart felt sudden, and how the equations let us predict its speed and distance at any moment.)

LESSONS.title: Problem Solving with the Equations of Linear Motion: Slowing Down and Going Upward
LESSONS.aresKeywords: equations of linear motion, sign convention, negative acceleration, deceleration, retardation, thrown upward, a = -10 m/s², multi-step problems, mkokoteni, boda-boda, Mombasa rooftop, Rift Valley runner

slo.purpose: Learners use the four equations of linear motion in multi-step problems. They apply a sign convention, handle negative acceleration (slowing down) and treat an object thrown upward under a = -10 m/s². This moves them toward predicting the runaway mkokoteni's motion and understanding free fall.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: calculate variables of motion using equations of linear motion with constant acceleration (v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u+v)t), including cases where acceleration is negative and where motion is vertical and upward (a = -10 m/s²).
slo.skills: Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking: listing knowns and the unknown, choosing an equation, and substituting with units. Analysing and Interpreting Data: checking answers against a second equation and against common sense. Constructing Explanations: defending a solution to the class. Communication and collaboration: presenting and critiquing solutions in groups.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the significance of linear motion in real life (the runner, the boda-boda, the thrown ball). Show Peace by staying calm and tolerant when peers challenge a solution. Show Unity by sharing roles in the group (reader, calculator, checker, presenter).
slo.keyInquiry: How is free fall motion important in real life? How can the dangers of free fall in our day-to-day life be mitigated? (Lesson focus: how do we correctly handle slowing down and upward motion so that the same equations that predict the runaway mkokoteni also predict a braking boda-boda and a ball thrown upward?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 2 gave learners the four equations and a method for choosing one. Lesson 3 stress-tests that method on harder cases: starting from rest, braking to a stop, and rising then falling. Learners see that one set of equations, with a clear sign convention, covers every constant-acceleration case. This prepares them to investigate free fall (Lesson 4) and to predict the mkokoteni at any moment, which is the driving question.
slo.safetyNotes: The Mombasa rooftop ball is a paper problem. Do not throw objects from roofs or windows. If you demonstrate an upward throw, use a soft ball outdoors in a cleared area, with learners standing well back and no one underneath. Keep walkways clear during group work and gallery walks. Remind learners that a real boda-boda must never be braked hard on a wet or loose-surface road without care, because that is a lesson in road safety, not an experiment.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the runaway mkokoteni on the Limuru escarpment. Mzee Kamau's loaded cart (300 kg) is released from rest and gains 2 m/s every second (a = 2.0 m/s²). Learners now ask what happens when acceleration is not a simple speed-up from rest. They predict answers to three Kenyan situations, then solve them in groups with a strategy: draw a sketch, choose the positive direction, list knowns and the unknown, choose an equation, solve, and check with a second equation. The problems are (a) a Rift Valley 400 m runner accelerating from rest, (b) boda-boda rider Otieno braking before a police check, and (c) a ball thrown upward from a 20 m Mombasa rooftop. Groups present on the board with cold-calling and a 30-second wait time. Learners then explain why the sign of acceleration matters, add new questions to the DQB, and add a sign-convention note to the class model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the runaway mkokoteni: released from rest, a = 2.0 m/s², 10 m/s after 5 s, 20 m/s (72 km/h) after 10 s and 100 m. They are shown three situations on the board: (a) a Rift Valley runner leaving the blocks in a 400 m race, (b) boda-boda rider Otieno braking from 15 m/s when he sees a police check, (c) a ball thrown upward at 15 m/s from a Mombasa rooftop 20 m above the ground. Individually, they write predictions in their journals: (1) Will the runner's speed after 2.5 s be less than, equal to, or more than 10 m/s? (2) Will Otieno's boda-boda stop in less than 20 m, about 40 m, or more than 60 m? (3) How long will the ball stay in the air, and will it hit the ground faster or slower than 15 m/s? Each learner gives a reason and a confidence rating from 1 to 5. They then share with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Remember Mzee Kamau's mkokoteni. It sped up by 2 metres per second every second. Today we meet situations where things slow down, or go up before they come down. Before any calculation, write what you think will happen." Read each scenario aloud slowly. After each question say: "Take 15 seconds of silent thinking time. Pens down until I say write." WAIT TIME: 15 seconds, then 1 minute to write. Do not confirm answers. Cold-call 4 learners with different predictions, using the name cards, and ask each: "What in the situation made you choose that?" Record the predictions in a tally on the board. Say: "We will come back to these predictions at the end."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Predict step) with a confidence rating. Committing to a prediction and a reason exposes preconceptions, such as 'negative acceleration means going backwards' or 'a thrown ball has zero acceleration at the top'. These are the ideas the later calculations will confirm or challenge.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check journals for a written prediction and reason for all three situations. Note how many learners (tally) believe the ball has no acceleration at its highest point, and how many believe slowing down means a negative speed. Look for learners who link braking to the mkokoteni in reverse. Learners who leave a reason blank get a prompt: "What do you know about how the cart's speed changed?"

framework.learnerExperience: Part 1 (10 min): The teacher models a 6-step strategy with the mkokoteni as a warm-up: (1) sketch, (2) choose positive direction (down the slope is positive, so a = +2 m/s²), (3) list u, v, a, s, t with signs and units, (4) mark the unknown, (5) choose the equation that contains the unknown and three knowns, (6) check with a second equation. Using t = 5 s, learners confirm v = 10 m/s and s = 25 m. Part 2 (30 min): In groups of 4 with roles (reader, recorder, calculator, checker), learners solve the Problem Set. (a) Runner: from rest, a = 4 m/s² for 2.5 s. Find v and s. (b) Boda-boda: u = 15 m/s, a = -3 m/s², finds the time to stop (v = 0) and the stopping distance. (c) Ball: thrown upward at u = +15 m/s from a 20 m rooftop, up is positive, a = -10 m/s². Find (i) the time to the highest point, (ii) the extra height risen, (iii) the maximum height above the ground, (iv) the time to reach the ground (s = -20 m), and (v) the impact velocity. Each group fills a solution sheet showing the sketch, knowns, equation, working and a check. Early finishers extend: compare with the mkokoteni by asking which of the three situations has acceleration in the same direction as the motion.
framework.teacherMoves: Model the strategy on the board with the mkokoteni, thinking aloud: "Down the slope is my positive direction, so a is plus 2." Then circulate with a checklist. Ask groups that are stuck: "What are your five variables? Which one do you not know? Which equation has the unknown and no other missing variable?" For (b) ask: "What is v when the boda-boda stops? Is a positive or negative, and why?" For (c) ask: "What is the velocity at the very top? What is the sign of a on the way up, at the top, and on the way down?" Give a hint card only after two attempts. Do not give final answers. WAIT TIME: after each question to a group, wait 10 seconds before adding a hint. Pause at 20 minutes and say: "Checkers, verify with a second equation, for example v² = u² + 2as." Keep time and remind: "Ball problem: you may not throw anything; this is on paper only."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Problem-Solving Protocol (Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking), with a Sign-Convention Sketch. A fixed routine forces learners to decide the positive direction first. This makes negative acceleration meaningful (the velocity decreases) rather than mysterious. Checking with a second equation builds the habit of validating a model's prediction, as will be needed for the mkokoteni.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether each group (i) draws a sketch with an arrow marking positive, (ii) writes a = -3 m/s² and a = -10 m/s² with the negative sign, (iii) writes v = 0 for stopping and at the top of the throw, and (iv) checks with a second equation. Expected values: (a) v = 10 m/s, s = 12.5 m; (b) t = 5 s, s = 37.5 m; (c) 1.5 s up, 11.25 m extra, 31.25 m maximum height, reaches the ground at t = 4 s, impact velocity -25 m/s. Tick a checklist per group. Note common errors: using +15 for a, treating -25 m/s as slower than 15 m/s, or forgetting that the rooftop displacement is -20 m, not +20 m.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group puts its solution to problems (a), (b) and (c) on a poster or the board. The class does a gallery walk, then whole-class presentations. For each problem, at least 3 groups are cold-called to present, ask questions and challenge each other. Learners then explain in their own words: (1) why is a negative for the boda-boda and for the ball, but positive for the mkokoteni? (2) Why does the ball take 1.5 s to rise but 4 s to reach the ground rather than 3 s? (3) What does the answer -25 m/s mean, and is it faster or slower than the initial 15 m/s? (4) How does Otieno's stopping distance connect to the dangers on a sloping road like the Limuru escarpment? Learners write a 3-sentence explanation using the words 'sign', 'direction' and 'acceleration', then compare their final answers with their Predict journals and mark each prediction as supported or revised.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Before any group speaks, everyone check your own working for 30 seconds." WAIT TIME: give 30 seconds of silent thinking before taking responses on each problem. Cold-call a minimum of 3 groups per problem using a random-name method: "Group 4, what answer did you get for the boda-boda stopping distance? Group 7, do you agree? Group 2, what equation did you use to check?" Compare any differing answers on the board and ask the class to find the error: "Where does the working differ?" Press for reasoning: "How do you know a is negative?" and "Why does the ball have a = -10 at the very top, where its velocity is zero?" Contrast with the mkokoteni: "On the slope a = +2 because the cart speeds up in the positive direction. Otieno slows in the positive direction, so a is negative." Pose the safety link: "If Otieno was travelling at 15 m/s but the police check was 30 m away, what happens?" (37.5 m needed, so he would not stop in time). Ask 3 learners to restate the sign rule in their own words. Avoid evaluating until at least 3 groups have spoken; thank groups for correcting errors.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Argumentation from Evidence (Engaging in Argument from Evidence) with a Cold-Call Share-Out. Groups defend a numerical answer with working. Comparing different answers for the same problem produces productive disagreement that exposes misconceptions about signs. Linking the three problems back to the mkokoteni shows that the equations and the sign convention are general, supporting transfer to new motion situations.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for learners who can say that negative acceleration means velocity is decreasing in the chosen positive direction, not that the object is moving backwards. Listen for a justification that the ball's total time is 4 s because it rises 1.5 s, then falls 31.25 m (and not 20 m) to the ground. Look for learners who can state that impact velocity is -25 m/s, meaning 25 m/s downward. Use a quick 3-question exit slip (individual): (1) Write the value of a for a ball thrown upward. (2) Write the value of v at the highest point. (3) In 'a = -3 m/s²', what does the minus sign tell us? Sort slips into 'secure', 'nearly', 'not yet' piles for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class DQB, started in Lesson 1 around the question: 'Why does a runaway mkokoteni on the Limuru escarpment keep getting faster, and how can we use mathematics to predict exactly how fast and how far it will travel before it crashes?' In pairs they: (1) put a tick on existing questions that today's work helps answer (for example, how can equations predict speed and distance?), (2) write new questions on sticky notes, such as: Why is the mkokoteni's a only 2 m/s² while the ball's a is 10 m/s²? If the ball is dropped from the roof instead of thrown, how long would it take? How far does a matatu travel when it brakes at speed? Could a driver stop a runaway cart by braking? Why does the ball hit the ground faster than it was thrown up? (3) Place new notes beside the categories 'equations', 'slowing down', 'going upward/free fall' and 'safety'. They also add one fact to the 'What we know' column.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at our board. Which questions did today's problems help us answer? Which new questions do you have?" Give pairs 3 minutes with sticky notes. WAIT TIME: 10 seconds of silent thinking before pairs write. Cold-call 3 pairs to read out a new question and say where to place it, asking: "What evidence from today made you ask this?" Use the 'free fall' notes to preview Lesson 4: "Several of you ask whether all objects fall at the same rate. We will test that next lesson." Group questions into themes, and explicitly mark questions answered by the equations and those that need investigation. Do not answer the new questions yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with Question Sorting (Asking Questions and Defining Problems). Sorting questions into themes shows learners how today's evidence connects to the driving question, tracks what is answered and not yet answered, and sets the direction of the remaining lessons (free fall, stopping distance, graphs).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each pair has at least one new question linked to today's work, and that questions go beyond recall (for example, 'why' or 'what if' questions). Note whether learners connect the negative-acceleration cases back to the mkokoteni. Success looks like a sticky note reading something like 'If the cart decelerated like the boda-boda, how far would it travel?' Tally question categories to decide what Lesson 4 should emphasise.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model of the mkokoteni (annotated diagram plus velocity-time graph begun in earlier lessons). Individually, then in groups, they add: (1) a sign-convention note: 'down the slope is positive, so a = +2.0 m/s²'; (2) a small annotated panel comparing the three situations: runner (a = +4 m/s²), boda-boda (a = -3 m/s²), and the thrown ball (a = -10 m/s² on the way up and down); (3) a note in the mkokoteni diagram that speeds up in the positive direction means a and v share the same sign, while slowing down means they have opposite signs. They write one 'rule of thumb' in their own words and one line of the 6-step strategy they will use in future problems. Finally they revisit their Predict journals and write: 'I used to think ... Now I think ...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Our model must explain more than the cart. Add what you learned today about direction and sign." Hand out the class model sheet and ask groups to add the sign-convention panel. WAIT TIME: 10 to 15 seconds of quiet thinking before writing the 'rule of thumb'. Cold-call 3 learners to read their rule of thumb, and ask the class to critique: "Does this rule work for the runner? For the ball at the top?" Point to the mkokoteni: "If someone had braked the cart hard, which sign would a have?" Close by saying: "Next lesson we investigate whether all objects fall with the same acceleration. Keep your ball-problem answers; we will compare."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Developing and Using Models (Cumulative Model Revision). Adding the sign-convention panel to the existing mkokoteni model turns the model into a general tool for all constant-acceleration motion. Comparing 'I used to think / Now I think' statements makes the revision of ideas explicit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each model includes (i) the positive direction marked, (ii) a = +2.0 m/s² for the cart, (iii) a = -3 m/s² for the boda-boda and a = -10 m/s² for the ball, and (iv) a sensible rule of thumb (a and v with opposite signs means slowing down). Collect the 'I used to think / Now I think' statements and look for at least one revised idea per learner.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Which sign-convention errors were most common (using +15 for a, -25 m/s seen as 'slower', forgetting s = -20 m for the rooftop)? (2) Did at least 3 groups present each problem, and did the 30-second wait time produce more reasoned answers? (3) Did learners link the boda-boda's stopping distance (37.5 m) to the dangers on a sloping road? (4) Which learners still treated the ball's top-of-flight acceleration as zero, and what additional task would help? (5) Did the group roles keep every learner working, or did the calculator dominate? (6) What should be adjusted before Lesson 4 (free fall investigation), where the sign convention for downward motion will be reused?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We solved the Problem Set. The Rift Valley runner reached 10 m/s after 2.5 s and covered 12.5 m. The boda-boda travelling at 15 m/s with a = -3 m/s² stopped after 5 s and 37.5 m. The ball thrown upward at 15 m/s from the 20 m Mombasa rooftop rose 11.25 m more in 1.5 s (31.25 m above the ground), reached the ground at t = 4 s and hit it at -25 m/s (25 m/s downward).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned to pick a positive direction first, list the knowns with signs, and choose the equation that has the unknown. Slowing down gives a negative a (opposite sign to v). For a ball thrown upward, a = -10 m/s² all the time, even at the top, where v = 0. The same equations work for speeding up, slowing down and vertical motion, just like for Mzee Kamau's mkokoteni (a = +2.0 m/s² down the slope).
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The mkokoteni keeps getting faster because its acceleration is in the same direction as its motion (a = +2.0 m/s² down the slope), so its velocity grows by 2 m/s every second. A braking boda-boda has a negative acceleration because it opposes the motion, so its velocity falls. Because acceleration is constant in each case, the equations of linear motion let us predict speed, distance and time at any moment, and a consistent sign convention is what makes these predictions correct.
