LESSONS.title: Investigating Free Fall: Predict and Observe
LESSONS.aresKeywords: free fall, gravity, acceleration due to gravity, g, air resistance, drop height, time of fall, s = ½at², reaction-time error, mkokoteni

slo.purpose: To gather first-hand evidence that all objects fall with the same acceleration when air resistance is negligible, and to estimate g from measured drop height and fall time. Free fall is the extreme case of the mkokoteni's situation: gravity pulling on a vertical path instead of a gentle slope.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) investigate the effect of gravity on bodies under free fall by dropping objects from a fixed height of 2.0 m; (b) state that when air resistance is negligible all objects fall with the same acceleration; (c) use g = 2h/t² (from s = ½at² with u = 0) to estimate g from class data (h = 2.0 m, mean t = 0.64 s, g = 9.8 m/s²); (d) explain why g = 10 m/s² is used in calculations.
slo.skills: Planning and carrying out investigations (NGSS SEP 3): controlling variables, repeating trials and measuring time with a stopwatch. Analysing and interpreting data (SEP 4): calculating means and g. Using mathematics (SEP 5): rearranging s = ½at² to g = 2h/t². Constructing explanations (SEP 6): inferring that gravity accelerates all objects equally. Evaluating error: reaction-time uncertainty.
slo.attitudes: Core competencies: Communication and collaboration (learners share roles and report data); Learning to learn (learners compare predictions with evidence and revise ideas). Values: Unity (cooperation while investigating the effect of gravity on objects); Peace (tolerance when predictions differ). PCIs: Life Skills Education (self-awareness: observing safety measures when dropping objects); Road safety (linking gravity on slopes to crashes).
slo.keyInquiry: KICD Key Inquiry Question 1: How is free fall motion important in real life? (Introduced here through evidence that gravity accelerates every object equally. Key Inquiry Question 2 on mitigating the dangers of free fall is addressed in later lessons.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 launched the mkokoteni puzzle and the idea that its velocity keeps increasing (it accelerates). Lesson 2 gave the four equations of linear motion, including s = ½at² with u = 0. Lesson 3 gave the sign convention and a = -10 m/s² for upward motion. In Lesson 4 learners collect their own evidence about gravity: do all objects speed up equally, and what is the value of g? This sets up Lesson 5, where g is applied to freely falling bodies and compared with the cart's slope acceleration of 2.0 m/s².
slo.safetyNotes: Drop from 2.0 m only over a cleared floor or soft sand tray. Use a rubber bung, stone and crumpled paper ball; keep the stone small (about the size of a mango seed). The dropper stands on a stable bench or the teacher stands on a stable chair or steps, with a spotter. Everyone else stands at least 1 m back. No one places hands or feet under a falling object. The stone is placed gently back by the timer after it comes to rest. Wear closed shoes. Spills or rolling objects are retrieved only after the trial is complete.

LESSONS.overview: The lesson returns to Mzee Kamau's runaway mkokoteni on the Limuru-Nairobi escarpment road: starting from rest, it reached 20 m/s (72 km/h) after 10 s and 100 m. Learners recall that gravity pulls it down the slope all the time. They then ask what happens when the slope is vertical, which is free fall. They first predict individually which of a ripe mango and a pebble hits the ground first and record the reasoning. In groups they drop a rubber bung, a stone and a crumpled paper ball from 2.0 m, time 5 trials each, and find the mean times: bung 0.63 s, stone 0.64 s, paper ball 0.65 s (mean 0.64 s). The times are almost identical, so the objects accelerate equally despite very different masses. Learners use s = ½at² with u = 0, rearranged to g = 2h/t², to estimate g = 4/0.64² = 9.8 m/s². They discuss reaction-time error and why calculations use g = 10 m/s² (theory gives t = 0.63 s). Learners add questions to the Driving Question Board and add free fall evidence to their draft model. The mkokoteni is not in free fall because the slope gives it only part of g; this is explored fully in Lesson 5.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 15 minutes) Learners recall the anchoring phenomenon: Mzee Kamau's loaded mkokoteni (300 kg) rolled down the Limuru-Nairobi escarpment and reached 20 m/s (72 km/h) after 10 s and 100 m. Achieng said, 'It started slowly then flew.' The teacher shows a ripe mango and a pebble held at shoulder height and asks: 'If the escarpment were vertical, like a cliff at Hell's Gate, and you dropped a ripe mango and a pebble from the same height, which hits the ground first?' Individually, in their science journals, learners write (1) their prediction (mango first, pebble first, or together), (2) a reason in one sentence, and (3) a quick sketch showing which object speeds up more. Then learners compare predictions with a partner and tally the class votes by raised hands. Common ideas are expected: heavier objects fall faster because gravity pulls harder on them. Learners also predict whether a crumpled paper ball and a flat sheet of paper will fall at the same rate, and why.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Remember Mzee Kamau's cart. Nothing pushed it, yet it kept getting faster. Today we ask what happens when the slope is as steep as it can possibly be.' Hold up the mango and the pebble. Do NOT drop them yet. Say: 'Write your prediction silently first. No talking for 2 minutes.' Circulate and note the reasons that learners give. Then ask for a show of hands for each option and record the vote on the board. Cold-call 3 learners with different predictions: 'Tell us your reason, not just your answer.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before calling on anyone. Say: 'Is it true that a heavier object has a bigger pull from gravity? Does a bigger pull mean a bigger speeding up? Hold that thought.' Do not correct any ideas. Say: 'Keep your predictions. We will test them with measurements.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with individual commitment: writing a prediction and reason before seeing evidence makes learners' current ideas visible, so that later conflict between prediction and data produces conceptual change. Think-Pair-Share lets learners rehearse and justify reasoning safely before public voting.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect journals and check each prediction for: (a) a clear choice, (b) a reason that mentions mass, size or air, and (c) a sketch. Indicators: learners who write that heavier objects fall faster hold the misconception to be revisited; learners who mention air or shape show useful ideas. Tally the vote on the board: expect a majority to choose the pebble or the heavier object. Note names of learners who predict 'together' to invite their reasoning later.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 30 minutes) In groups of 5 with assigned roles (dropper, timer, spotter, recorder, reporter), learners test their predictions. Equipment: a metre rule or tape and string to mark a fixed drop height of h = 2.0 m (measured from the bottom of the object to the floor), a stopwatch or phone timer, a rubber bung, a small stone and a crumpled paper ball. They also drop a flat sheet of paper beside a crumpled one as a fair test of shape. For each of the three objects they drop 5 times from 2.0 m, time each fall, and record in a table: object, trial 1 to 5, mean time. The class data are collected on the board: rubber bung mean 0.63 s, stone 0.64 s, crumpled paper ball 0.65 s; mean of all three 0.64 s. Learners notice that the times differ by only 0.01 to 0.02 s even though the stone is much heavier than the paper. They discuss what makes timing difficult (reaction time of about 0.1 to 0.2 s when starting and stopping the watch) and why repeating trials and averaging helps. The flat sheet falls much slower than the crumpled ball, which they note as an air-resistance effect.
framework.teacherMoves: Demonstrate safe dropping first: 'Stand behind the line. The dropper releases, does not throw. Spotter, your job is to watch the floor area.' Say: 'Fair test: what must we keep the same?' Cold-call 2 learners (height, release method). Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Show how to release both objects at once from the same height and ask learners to listen for the landing sounds: 'Do you hear one thud or two?' Move among groups asking: 'Which object do you expect to take longest? Does your table show that?' When groups finish, collect the means on the board with the reporter from each group. Say: 'Notice the numbers: 0.63, 0.64, 0.65. Why are they so close when a stone is far heavier than paper?' Wait 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Ask: 'Why did the flat paper fall slowly? What is different about the crumpled ball?' Enforce safety: 'No hands or feet under the drop.' Point out that this is the same gravity that pulls Mzee Kamau's cart: 'On the slope it pulls along the road. Here it pulls straight down.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table and pattern-finding with controlled variables: holding the height constant and varying only the object isolates the effect of mass and shape, and repeated trials with averaging teach how to handle measurement uncertainty. Error discussion helps learners distinguish a real difference from reaction-time noise.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether each group (a) measures a 2.0 m height accurately, (b) releases objects without pushing, (c) records 5 trials for each object, and (d) calculates means correctly. Indicators: learners say that 0.01 to 0.02 s differences are within reaction-time error; learners keep the height the same for all trials. Ask each recorder to show the table: a complete table with units (s) shows readiness. Look for learners who use air resistance to explain the flat sheet.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 20 minutes) Learners use the class data to explain what they saw and to calculate g. Step 1: They state a claim in their journals: 'All three objects reached the ground at about the same time, so gravity gives them the same acceleration (mass does not matter) when air resistance is negligible.' Step 2: Using Lesson 2's s = ½at² with u = 0 and the sign convention from Lesson 3 (down taken as positive, so a = +g), they rearrange to g = 2h/t². Step 3: They substitute the class mean: g = 2 x 2.0 / 0.64² = 4 / 0.4096 = 9.8 m/s² (2 s.f.). Step 4: They compare with theory using g = 10 m/s²: t = sqrt(2h/g) = sqrt(0.4) = 0.63 s, which is within reaction-time error of 0.64 s. They are told that calculations in this course use g = 10 m/s², and that 9.8 m/s² is the measured value. Step 5: They connect to the phenomenon: every second in free fall adds about 10 m/s to the speed, so a vertical drop of 20 m takes only 2 s, whereas the cart on the gentle escarpment slope had to travel 100 m. They write one sentence on why the mkokoteni's acceleration is smaller than g (the slope reduces the pull along the road) as a prediction to be examined in Lesson 5.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Here is the claim we will test with the evidence: all objects fall with the same acceleration when air resistance is negligible.' Ask learners to write the claim and the evidence from the table. Cold-call 3 learners to state the evidence aloud. Write s = ½at² on the board and ask: 'Our object starts from rest, so u = 0. If a is g and s is h, what does the equation become?' Wait 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners and write g = 2h/t². Walk through the substitution in steps on the board, with units, and have learners do the arithmetic in pairs (4 / 0.4096). Ask: 'Our g is 9.8 and the textbook uses 10. Is our experiment wrong?' Wait 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to discuss reaction time, rounding and air resistance. Say: 'In this course we use g = 10 m/s², so exercises are clean.' Ask: 'The mass of the cart was 300 kg. Did that change how it accelerated? What does today's evidence suggest?' Wait 10-15 seconds and cold-call 2 learners. Link to the road: 'On the cliff the pull is the whole of g. On the escarpment, only part of it.' Do not teach the 0.2 fraction calculation (Lesson 5).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER): learners state the claim, cite their class data and justify with the equation s = ½at², so the conclusion is built from evidence and mathematics instead of authority. Reusing earlier equations (Lesson 2) shows how a measurement turns into a physical constant.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check journals for: (a) a claim that matches the evidence, (b) citations of the numbers (0.63, 0.64, 0.65 s), (c) correct rearrangement g = 2h/t², and (d) a calculated g near 9.8 m/s² with units. Indicators: learners explain that differences are within reaction-time error; learners say that the mass of the object does not change the acceleration; learners do not say that heavier objects fall faster. Ask 3 learners to calculate g for a single time (for example, 0.65 s gives 9.5 m/s²) on mini-whiteboards and hold them up for a quick scan.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 8 minutes) Learners return to the class Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1: 'Why does a runaway mkokoteni on the Limuru escarpment keep getting faster, and how can we use mathematics to predict exactly how fast and how far it will travel before it crashes?' On sticky notes, each learner writes one new question or partial answer from today's evidence, for example: 'If gravity gives every object the same acceleration, why does the cart accelerate at only 2 m/s²?' 'Why did the flat paper fall slowly?' 'How fast would an object be moving after 2 s in free fall?' 'Could we use free fall to predict how far something drops?' They place notes under headings: Answered, Partly answered and New questions. Learners also move the Lesson 4 notes on gravity to the 'Partly answered' section of the DQB, marking what is known (gravity accelerates all objects equally; g is about 10 m/s²) and what is not yet known (how the slope changes the acceleration).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take one sticky note. Write a question that today's drops make you wonder about, or an answer you can now give to a question already on the board.' Give 2 minutes of silent writing. Invite 4 learners to read their notes and place them. Ask: 'Which question on the board does today's evidence help answer?' Wait 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners. Point to any question about why the cart's acceleration is not as big as g and say: 'This is a question we will answer in Lesson 5.' Highlight questions about air resistance and say: 'Good, we ignore it for now but we must keep it in mind.' Move answered notes into the correct column and thank learners for the question.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: a public record that shows how each piece of evidence moves the class from puzzlement to explanation, giving learners ownership of the questions and signalling what has yet to be explained.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check sticky notes for questions that link free fall to the mkokoteni, the slope or air resistance. Indicators: at least 80 percent of learners submit a question or answer; notes refer to evidence (for example '0.64 s') instead of vague statements; some learners link to Lesson 2's equation or Lesson 3's sign convention. Notice learners who still ask whether heavier objects fall faster; follow up with them individually.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 7 minutes) Learners open their draft model for the cart, an annotated diagram of the cart on the escarpment, which in Lesson 7 will be completed with a velocity-time graph. They add a 'Free fall evidence' panel. It has a vertical arrow showing an object dropped from 2.0 m, the label 'a = g = 10 m/s² downward (measured 9.8 m/s²)', the relation g = 2h/t², and the note 'mass does not change the acceleration when air resistance is negligible'. Beside the cart drawing they add a question mark note: 'The slope gives a smaller acceleration than g. How much smaller?' They also add a mini table of the cart's first rows from earlier lessons (t = 1 s: v = 2 m/s, s = 1 m) next to the idea that free fall would give v = 10 m/s after 1 s, as a prediction for comparison. They reflect in one sentence: 'Today I learned that ___, which helps explain the mkokoteni because ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your model. Add a panel for free fall.' Show an example on the board: an arrow down, a = g, and the note about mass. Ask: 'Where on your model does gravity act on the cart? In which direction?' Wait 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 2 learners. Say: 'The cart is not in free fall. What do you think is different?' Take 3 responses and accept ideas about the slope without confirming. Say: 'In the next lesson we will use numbers to test your idea.' Circulate and check that each model uses units and the sign convention (down positive). Remind learners to keep models for Lesson 7.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model building: adding each new piece of evidence to one visual model lets learners integrate ideas across lessons and notice gaps (here, how slope affects acceleration), which maintains coherence in the storyline.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check models for: (a) a free fall panel with g = 10 m/s² and the equation g = 2h/t², (b) a statement that mass does not change acceleration, (c) a sensible question about the slope, and (d) units on all numbers. Indicators of understanding: the learner connects gravity to the cart's steady increase in velocity; the learner does not claim the cart accelerates at 10 m/s². Use the reflection sentence as an exit ticket and sort it into 'got it', 'nearly' and 'needs support' for follow-up in Lesson 5.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson consider: (1) How many learners changed their prediction after seeing the three class means of 0.63, 0.64 and 0.65 s, and which reasons did the learners who did not change give? (2) Did groups control the 2.0 m height and release method, and how reliable were their stopwatch times? (3) Could learners explain why 9.8 m/s² and 10 m/s² are both acceptable, and did anyone treat the difference as an error in the experiment? (4) Did learners confuse the stone and the crumpled paper ball results with the flat sheet and air resistance? (5) Did learners apply s = ½at² with u = 0 correctly and use the sign convention from Lesson 3? (6) What misconceptions about heavier objects remain, and how will you address them in Lesson 5? (7) Were safety rules followed during dropping? Record any adjustments to apparatus (for example, a phone slow-motion video for timing) for future lessons.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We dropped a rubber bung, a stone and a crumpled paper ball from 2.0 m. Mean fall times were 0.63 s, 0.64 s and 0.65 s (class mean 0.64 s), almost the same although the masses were very different. A flat sheet of paper fell more slowly than the crumpled ball.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: When air resistance is negligible, all objects fall with the same acceleration due to gravity, regardless of mass. Using s = ½at² with u = 0, g = 2h/t² = 4/0.64² = 9.8 m/s², and we use g = 10 m/s² in calculations. Differences are within reaction-time error.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Gravity pulls on the mkokoteni all the time, so it keeps getting faster, and free fall shows what gravity does on a vertical path: every second adds about 10 m/s to the speed of any object. The cart on the escarpment is not in free fall, so its acceleration is smaller than g (to be investigated in Lesson 5), but the same equations apply to predict its speed and distance.

LESSONS.title: Freely Falling Bodies: Explain and Calculate
LESSONS.aresKeywords: free fall, acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m/s², equations of linear motion, mkokoteni, escarpment slope, sin(angle) = 0.2, impact speed, drop height, road safety

slo.purpose: Learners apply the equations of linear motion with u = 0 and a = g = 10 m/s² to free-fall problems, and explain why the slope reduces the mkokoteni's acceleration to a = g x 0.2 = 2.0 m/s², so that the cart and a free-falling body can reach the same 20 m/s in very different times.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) calculate variables of motion using equations of linear motion with constant acceleration (v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u+v)t); (b) investigate the effect of gravity on bodies under free fall, using the class data from Lesson 4 (g estimated as 9.8 m/s², exercises use g = 10 m/s²); (c) appreciate the significance of linear motion and free fall in real life. Learners will also state that the mkokoteni is NOT in free fall: its acceleration along the slope is g x 0.2 = 2 m/s², while free fall on a vertical path has a = g = 10 m/s².
slo.skills: Critical thinking and problem solving (listing knowns and unknowns, choosing an equation, using the sign convention); communication and collaboration (explaining calculation steps to peers); learning to learn (reflecting on the Lesson 4 data and on predictions). NGSS practices: Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking; Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Constructing Explanations; Developing and Using Models.
slo.attitudes: Values: Peace (displaying tolerance and calmness when discussing applications of linear motion in real life); Unity (cooperating with others while working on the calculations). PCIs: Road safety (increased awareness of how to minimise fatal injuries resulting from road crashes on sloping roads using the concept of free fall of objects); Life Skills Education (self-awareness) (observing safety measures when objects are dropped). Learners show respect for peers' reasoning and appreciate how mathematics lets us predict danger before it happens.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How is free fall motion important in real life? 2. How can the dangers of free fall in our day-to-day life be mitigated?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 4 gave the class a measured g (9.8 m/s² from h = 2.0 m and a mean time of 0.64 s). Lesson 5 turns that evidence into prediction: learners use u = 0 and a = g to calculate for a mango, then a 45 m drop, and then compare free fall with the mkokoteni on the escarpment. The key insight is that the cart reaches the same 20 m/s as a 20 m free fall but needs 10 s instead of 2 s, because the slope supplies only 0.2 of g. This links to the DQB and sets up Lesson 6 (stopping distances) and Lesson 7 (velocity-time graph).
slo.safetyNotes: This is a calculation lesson; no drops are required. If learners re-demonstrate any drop for the DQB, drop only light objects (rubber bung, paper ball) from no more than 2 m, with the area below cleared, and nobody standing underneath. Learners must NOT drop anything from a window, a building or a tree, and must not climb anything. No real mkokoteni or vehicle is to be released on any slope; the escarpment scenario is worked on paper only. Keep feet clear of the demonstration area and report any accident to the teacher at once.

LESSONS.overview: Learners recall the Mzee Kamau scenario: a loaded mkokoteni (300 kg) released from rest at the top of a steep 100 m section of the Limuru-Nairobi escarpment road crashes into a parked lorry at 20 m/s (72 km/h) after 10 s, and Achieng says 'it started slowly then flew'. They first predict the mango fall time and the drop height for a 30 m/s impact, then review the Lesson 4 data (g = 9.8 m/s² estimated; g = 10 m/s² used for calculation). In the Observe phase they work through three calculations as evidence: (a) a mango falling from a 5 m branch in a school compound (t = 1 s, v = 10 m/s); (b) an object hitting the ground at 30 m/s (dropped from 45 m, falling for 3 s); (c) the cart at s = 25 m, using a = 2 and not 10 (v = 10 m/s, t = 5 s). In the Explain phase they compare a 20 m free fall (2 s, 20 m/s) with the cart (10 s, 20 m/s) and explain that the slope gives only 0.2 of g, and that free fall is the extreme case of a vertical slope. They then discuss dangers on steep roads and ways to reduce them, update the DQB and revise the class model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in groups of four. They look at the sketch of the escarpment (100 m road, 20 m vertical drop, lorry at the bottom) and the sketch of a mango tree in a school compound with a 5 m branch. Individually, in their notebooks, they write predictions for three questions: (1) How long will a mango take to fall from the 5 m branch, and how fast will it be going when it lands? (2) An object hits the ground at 30 m/s: from what height was it dropped? (3) If the cart fell vertically through 20 m instead of rolling down the slope, would it reach the bottom sooner or later than 10 s, and would its final speed be bigger, smaller or the same as 20 m/s? They give a reason for each prediction and rate their confidence (1-3). Groups then share predictions and sketch them as quick estimates on a sheet of paper. Predictions link to the phenomenon: the cart gets faster because gravity keeps pulling it down the slope.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the escarpment sketch and say: 'Remember Mzee Kamau's cart. Achieng said it started slowly then flew. Today we turn Lesson 4's measured g into predictions.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing: 'Write your own prediction first. No talking yet.' Then say: 'Before we calculate anything, what do you think?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners (from different groups) for question 1, and 3 learners for question 3, asking each: 'What is your reason?' Do NOT confirm or correct. Record the class predictions in a tally on the board (sooner / later / same). Say: 'Keep your predictions. We will test them with numbers.' Circulate and note common ideas such as 'heavier things fall faster' or 'free fall is the same as the cart'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-with-reasons (eliciting prior ideas): writing a prediction and a reason before any calculation makes learners commit to an idea, so that later evidence either supports it or creates productive conflict. The confidence rating lets learners see how their certainty changes with evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) every learner has written a prediction and a reason for all three questions; (2) teacher tallies how many predict 'later' for the free-fall time compared with the cart (the correct idea) vs 'sooner' or 'same'; (3) teacher listens for the misconception that the cart's mass or load of maize changes its acceleration, or that the cart is in free fall; (4) at least 4 different learners voice reasoning in the cold calls.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners gather evidence in two steps. Step 1: Recall the Lesson 4 data (h = 2.0 m; mean times: rubber bung 0.63 s, stone 0.64 s, paper ball 0.65 s; mean 0.64 s). They recompute g = 2h/t² = 4/0.64² = 4/0.4096 = 9.8 m/s² and note that theory with g = 10 gives t = sqrt(0.4) = 0.63 s, and that the differences are within reaction-time error. They agree to use g = 10 m/s² in the exercises. Step 2: In groups, they work through three calculations on a worksheet, writing known values (u, a, s, v, t), choosing an equation and giving units. Down is positive. (a) Mango from a 5 m branch: u = 0, a = 10, s = 5 so s = ½at² gives 5 = 5t², t = 1 s, then v = u + at = 10 m/s. (b) Object hits the ground at 30 m/s: u = 0, v = 30, a = 10, so s = v²/2g = 900/20 = 45 m, and t = v/a = 3 s. (c) The cart at s = 25 m on the slope: u = 0, a = 2 (NOT 10), v² = 2as = 2 x 2 x 25 = 100, so v = 10 m/s, and t = v/a = 5 s. They check (c) against the mkokoteni table (t = 5 s: v = 10 m/s, s = 25 m). Each group fills in a results table and cross-checks answers with a neighbouring group.
framework.teacherMoves: Give out worksheets. Say: 'First, list what you know and what you want. Which equation has exactly those variables?' Remind learners that Lesson 2 taught choosing an equation from the knowns and Lesson 3 taught the sign convention. Write on the board: 'List u, v, a, s, t. Mark the unknown. Pick the equation.' Circulate with these prompts: 'Why is u = 0 here?' 'Why a = 10 for the mango but a = 2 for the cart?' 'What are your units?' For calculation (c), stop the class and ask: 'The cart weighs 300 kg. The mango is much lighter. Does the cart accelerate faster?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Prompt: 'Does mass appear in any of the four equations?' Make sure every group finishes (a) before (b), and (b) before (c). Do not give answers; let groups check each other's results. After 20 minutes, record each group's answers on the board and mark any disagreement for discussion.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data-based reasoning with a structured problem-solving routine (known-unknown-equation-check): using the same steps for every problem lets learners focus on the physics, not on guessing. Comparing the cart's calculation with the mkokoteni table (a data check) builds confidence that the equations predict real motion, and the contrast between a = 10 and a = 2 exposes the role of the slope.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners list knowns and unknowns before computing; (2) correct answers: (a) t = 1 s and v = 10 m/s; (b) h = 45 m and t = 3 s; (c) v = 10 m/s and t = 5 s, with units; (3) learners use a = 2 for the cart and not 10; (4) learners can say that mass does not appear in the equations for free fall and does not change the cart's acceleration; (5) teacher notes which groups confuse g = 9.8 and g = 10 and reminds them that exercises use g = 10 m/s².

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their results to explain the phenomenon. Task 1 (free fall vs cart): they calculate a 20 m free fall: u = 0, a = 10, s = 20, so t = sqrt(2 x 20/10) = 2 s and v = 10 x 2 = 20 m/s. They put it side by side with the cart (10 s, 20 m/s) in a two-column table, and find that the final speeds are the same (20 m/s = 72 km/h) while the times differ (2 s vs 10 s). Task 2 (why the slope matters): they compute the ratio of accelerations 2/10 = 0.2 and relate it to sin(angle) = 0.2, i.e. the vertical drop of 0.2 m per metre travelled; they write in their own words: 'The slope gives the cart only 0.2 of g. A vertical path (sin = 1) gives a = g, so free fall is the extreme case of a slope.' Task 3 (explaining Achieng's 'started slowly then flew'): they use v = 2t and s = t² to explain that velocity begins at 0 and rises by 2 m/s every second, and that the distance grows as t² (25 m by 5 s, but 100 m by 10 s, so 75 m in the last 5 s). Task 4 (dangers and mitigation): in groups they discuss, for Key Inquiry 1 and 2, where free fall matters in real life (a mango falling, objects falling from scaffolding at a Nairobi construction site, a parked vehicle rolling downhill) and how dangers are reduced (escape lanes, warning signs on steep roads such as the Kinangop descent, wheel chocks, handbrakes, hard hats). Each group presents one claim with evidence from the calculations.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'We have two motions that end at the same speed. Why does one take 2 seconds and the other 10?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds and take no hands. Cold-call 3 learners one after another, each adding to the previous answer: 'Add to what she said.' Push for evidence: 'Which number shows that? Where is it in your table?' Ask: 'If the slope were twice as steep, what happens to a? What if it were vertical?' Draw an escarpment triangle and a vertical line on the board. Challenge the idea that the cart is in free fall: 'The cart has no engine and nobody pushes it. Is it in free fall? Why not?' (Free fall is motion under gravity alone along a vertical path with negligible air resistance; the cart is on a slope and the road holds part of the pull.) Use the road-safety discussion: 'Mzee Kamau's cart reached 72 km/h in 10 s. What could reduce the danger?' Take answers from 4 groups and press them to link each safety measure to the physics (e.g. a wheel chock stops acceleration from starting; an escape lane gives a long distance to stop). Do not teach stopping distance in detail; say: 'Lesson 6 will measure stopping distances.' Do not re-teach graphs; Lesson 7 covers them.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with a compare-and-contrast table: learners state a claim ('the slope reduces the cart's acceleration to 0.2 g'), cite numbers (2 s vs 10 s, 20 m/s vs 20 m/s) and give the reasoning (only part of gravity acts along the slope; a vertical path gives full g). Contrasting two cases of the same physics shows that free fall and the cart follow one set of equations, differing only in a.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners correctly state t = 2 s and v = 20 m/s for the 20 m free fall; (2) learners explain that the final speed is the same but the time is different because the slope gives a = 2 m/s², which is 0.2 of g; (3) learners say the cart is not in free fall; (4) learners link 'started slowly then flew' to v = 2t and s = t² using numbers (e.g. 25 m at 5 s, 100 m at 10 s); (5) learners name at least one real-life importance of free fall and one way of reducing danger; (6) at least 6 different learners speak during the discussion.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1. In groups, they (1) place sticky notes with answers for questions that can now be answered (e.g. 'Why does the cart keep getting faster with no one pushing?' - Gravity pulls it down the slope all the time, so a = 2 m/s² and v rises 2 m/s each second; 'Could we have predicted the speed?' - Yes, v = 2t gives 20 m/s at 10 s and v² = 2as gives 20 m/s at 100 m); (2) write at least one new question arising from today's work, such as 'Why does doubling speed make stopping so much harder?', 'What does the graph of the cart's motion look like?' or 'Does air resistance matter when a mango falls?'; and (3) move any answered question to the 'Answered' column, writing the evidence (calculation) on the note. They mark questions still open for later lessons.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which questions can we now answer with numbers, not just opinions?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Invite 3 groups to place and defend one answered note, asking 'What evidence supports it?' Say: 'Write one new question that today's work made you ask.' Cold-call 3 learners to read new questions aloud. Sort new questions: stopping distance and speed ones are linked to Lesson 6; graph questions are linked to Lesson 7. Do not answer them now. Point out any question about whether mass changes the cart's acceleration and ask learners to cite the calculation for the answer. Photograph or keep the DQB for the next lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding: moving questions from 'open' to 'answered' with evidence shows progress and motivates the next lessons, while new questions keep learning driven by the phenomenon and by learners' own curiosity.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) each group moves at least one question to 'Answered' and writes evidence with numbers; (2) each group writes at least one new, relevant question; (3) learners use terms such as acceleration, free fall, g and the equations correctly; (4) teacher notes which learners still ask about mass or 'weight making it faster' and plans a quick follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model of the mkokoteni (an annotated diagram; the velocity-time graph is built in Lesson 7). On the diagram of the 100 m escarpment road they (1) label the slope (sin = 0.2; 20 m vertical drop), the force of gravity, the direction of motion and a = 2.0 m/s²; (2) add speeds at t = 0, 2, 5 and 10 s (0, 4, 10, 20 m/s) and distances (0, 4, 25, 100 m) from the table; (3) add a small second sketch of the 20 m vertical free fall with a = g = 10 m/s², t = 2 s, v = 20 m/s; (4) write a caption: 'Free fall is the extreme case of a vertical slope; the slope reduces a to 0.2 g, so the cart takes 10 s but reaches the same 20 m/s'; and (5) write a safety note linking speed to danger on steep roads. They compare their revised model with their Lesson 1 model and note what has changed.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add today's evidence to your model. Where does g appear? Where does 0.2 appear?' Circulate and ask: 'How does your model show why the cart starts slowly?' 'How does it show that free fall is different from the cart?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 learners to explain one revision and the reason for it. Ask 2 pairs to swap models and give one piece of 'two stars and a wish' feedback. Use the check: 'If a = 2, what is v at 3 s?' (6 m/s) Collect models and note gaps (e.g. use of a = 10 for the cart). Finish by asking each learner to complete the summary table in the notebook: what we observed, what we learned, how we can explain it.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: learners add evidence and mathematical relationships to an annotated diagram, and so connect observations (the cart gets faster), mechanism (gravity along the slope, a = g x 0.2) and prediction (equations of linear motion). Comparing with the earlier model makes learning visible and builds the explanation for the final synthesis in Lesson 8.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) the model shows a = 2.0 m/s² for the cart and a = g = 10 m/s² for free fall, with no confusion between them; (2) speeds and distances at 2, 5 and 10 s match the table (4, 10, 20 m/s; 4, 25, 100 m); (3) the caption explains that the slope gives 0.2 of g; (4) the model includes a link to danger and road safety; (5) learners can explain one revision to the model and justify it with a calculation.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did learners choose equations by listing knowns and unknowns, or did they guess? Which groups needed help? (2) How many learners still think the cart is in free fall or that its 300 kg load changes its acceleration? What evidence from the calculations changed their minds? (3) Did learners distinguish g = 9.8 m/s² (measured in Lesson 4) from g = 10 m/s² (used in exercises) and explain why? (4) Was the comparison of 2 s and 10 s with the same 20 m/s clear? Which wording or sketch helped most? (5) Did the road-safety discussion connect to the physics and to local roads (Limuru, Kinangop descent), and were all learners able to contribute? (6) Which new DQB questions should be used in Lesson 6 (stopping distance) and Lesson 7 (graphs)? What adjustments are needed to the timing, grouping or worksheet?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe and calculate today? (Include: the mango from the 5 m branch takes t = 1 s and lands at v = 10 m/s; an object hitting the ground at 30 m/s was dropped from 45 m and fell for 3 s; the cart at s = 25 m has v = 10 m/s after t = 5 s; a 20 m free fall takes 2 s and gives 20 m/s while the cart takes 10 s for the same 20 m/s.)
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we learn? (Include: with u = 0 and a = g = 10 m/s², the equations of linear motion predict time, speed and height for freely falling bodies; mass does not change the acceleration; the mkokoteni is not in free fall because on the slope its acceleration is g x 0.2 = 2 m/s²; free fall is the extreme case of a vertical slope.)
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How can we now explain the phenomenon? (Include: the cart keeps getting faster because gravity pulls it down the slope all the time, so its velocity rises by 2 m/s every second; it starts slowly because velocity begins at zero and feels sudden because distance grows as t²; the same equations predict 20 m/s (72 km/h) after 10 s and 100 m, and show why steep roads are dangerous.)
