LESSONS.title: Road Safety: Stopping Distance and Real-Life Applications of Linear Motion
LESSONS.aresKeywords: stopping distance, reaction distance, braking distance, deceleration, v² = u² + 2as, Mombasa Road, Kinangop descent, NTSA, road safety, mkokoteni

slo.purpose: Learners use the equations of linear motion to explain why a runaway mkokoteni hits a lorry at 20 m/s, and why higher speeds on roads like Mombasa Road need far longer stopping distances. They connect the physics to NTSA road-safety rules and to one further application of linear motion in Kenya.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) explain that stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance; (b) calculate braking distance using v² = u² + 2as with v = 0 and a = -5 m/s² (dry) or -2.5 m/s² (wet); (c) show that braking distance depends on the square of speed (braking distance = u²/2|a|), so doubling the speed multiplies it by 4 and tripling it by 9; (d) discuss the dangers of accelerating on steeply sloping roads and the safety measures used to reduce fatal injuries; (e) appreciate the significance of linear motion in real life.
slo.skills: Calculating with the equations of linear motion (NGSS: Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking); analysing and interpreting data from a table (NGSS: Analyzing and Interpreting Data); constructing explanations from evidence (NGSS: Constructing Explanations); researching with digital or print media and presenting findings in a group (Communication and collaboration).
slo.attitudes: Learners value road safety and take responsibility for safe behaviour as passengers, pedestrians and drivers. Peace: they stay calm and tolerant when discussing applications. Unity: they cooperate in group research. Respect: they value others' opinions when debating road-safety rules.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How is free fall motion important in real life? 2. How can the dangers of free fall in our day-to-day life be mitigated?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 to 5 showed that the mkokoteni accelerates at a constant 2.0 m/s² and reaches 20 m/s (72 km/h) after 10 s and 100 m, and that free fall is the same physics with a = g. Lesson 6 turns this knowledge to the other side of the problem: how far does a vehicle travel while stopping? It moves the driving question from predicting speed and distance to using that prediction to save lives. Learners see that speed matters most because distance depends on v². Lesson 7 will then bring everything together on the velocity-time graph model.
slo.safetyNotes: Do the stopping-distance activity on the school field or in the corridor, never on a real road. Use chalk or string for the marked distances, and keep walking-pace trials away from other learners. Keep the cart demonstration to a small toy or trolley on a short plank, with a box to catch it. Learners using digital devices must follow the school rules on safe use and online safety. Treat discussion of road crashes sensitively, since some learners may have been affected by one.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by predicting how far a matatu on Mombasa Road needs to stop when it is travelling at 36, 72 and 108 km/h, and whether doubling the speed doubles the distance. In the Observe Phase they find the answer in a data table. They convert the speeds to 10, 20 and 30 m/s, calculate reaction distance (speed x 1.0 s) and braking distance (v² = u² + 2as with v = 0, a = -5 m/s² dry and -2.5 m/s² wet), and compare the results. In the Explain Phase they link the results to the mkokoteni, which has no brakes and ends at 20 m/s, to the dangers of speed on slopes, and to Kinangop descent signs and NTSA guidelines. They then research one other Kenyan application of linear motion (SGR train, pole vault or construction safety) for a presentation in Lesson 7. The lesson ends by updating the DQB and the class model.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners recall the mkokoteni crashing into the parked lorry at 20 m/s (72 km/h) and are shown a sketch of a matatu on Mombasa Road with a boy stepping onto the road ahead. Individually they answer on paper: (1) What two things happen between the driver seeing danger and the matatu stopping? (2) If the matatu is at 36 km/h and needs about 20 m to stop, how far will it need at 72 km/h and at 108 km/h? They write a number and a reason for each, then sketch a quick bar or distance line for the three speeds. They then share with a partner and note where they disagree. Most will predict 40 m and 60 m (a doubling and a tripling), a useful misconception to test.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Last lesson, our mkokoteni had no brakes and no driver. Today the matatu has both. Think about Mombasa Road. Between the driver seeing danger and the matatu coming to a stop, what happens?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds in silence before anyone speaks. Then say: "Write your prediction for 72 km/h and 108 km/h. Do not worry about being right; I want your reasoning." Walk around and cold-call 4 learners to give their numbers and reasons, without saying who is right. Record the predictions on the board in a table headed "Prediction before evidence" so they can be compared later. Ask: "Who predicted the distance doubles when the speed doubles? Hands up. Who thinks it might be more than double?" Count hands and write the counts down. Do not correct anyone; say: "We will test that with evidence in a moment."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction stage). Committing to a written prediction and reason makes learners aware of their own idea (distance is proportional to speed), so the evidence later produces a real cognitive conflict instead of being passively received. Cold-calling shows learners that the class holds several different ideas.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the written predictions. Look for: (a) whether learners identify two stages (reaction time and braking); (b) whether they predict a linear pattern (40 m, 60 m) or a faster growth; (c) whether they link the distance to the speed using ideas from Lesson 3. Tally the hand counts. Note learners who give no reasoning and return to them in the Observe Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) In groups of 4, learners get the Stopping Distance Data Sheet for a matatu on Mombasa Road (driver reaction time 1.0 s; braking deceleration 5 m/s² on dry road and 2.5 m/s² on wet road). Part A (10 min): they convert 36, 72 and 108 km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6 (10, 20, 30 m/s). Reaction distance = speed x 1.0 s gives 10 m, 20 m and 30 m. Part B (10 min): for braking distance they use equation (3), v² = u² + 2as, with v = 0 and a = -5 m/s²: 0 = u² - 10s, so s = u²/10. Dry road: 10 m, 40 m, 90 m. Wet road with a = -2.5 m/s²: 20 m, 80 m, 180 m. They complete the table: total stopping distance on the dry road is 20 m at 10 m/s, 60 m at 20 m/s and 120 m at 30 m/s. Part C (5 min): they compare their numbers with their predictions and look for a pattern in the braking column, e.g. 10 to 40 to 90 (x1, x4, x9). Practical option on the school field: learners mark out 10 m, 20 m and 30 m with chalk and walk them at steady pace, counting 1 second per 'step' to feel what 'reaction distance' means.
framework.teacherMoves: Hand out the data sheets and say: "Convert first. Dividing by 3.6 gives metres per second. Check with your partner before you go on." Circulate and look for the common mistake of using a = +5 instead of -5 or forgetting that v = 0. Say: "Which equation has no time in it? Why is that the one we want?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups to explain their choice of v² = u² + 2as. Say: "Look at the 72 km/h row. The speed is double the first row. What happened to the reaction distance? What happened to the braking distance?" Cold-call 4 learners for their results. Do not give the pattern; ask: "Look down the braking column: 10, 40, 90. What is the pattern?" WAIT TIME 15 seconds. If learners are stuck, prompt: "Compare it with 1, 2, 3 for the speeds." Remind them to keep the units (m, s, m/s, m/s²) in every line. Check that every group has the reaction distance, braking distance and total for both road conditions.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table analysis with pattern finding. Learners produce the data themselves from the equations of linear motion and then look for relationships (reaction distance is proportional to speed; braking distance is proportional to speed squared). Calculating the numbers first and then spotting the pattern builds a deeper understanding than being told that distance goes with v².
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) learners write a = -5 m/s² as negative; (b) they use v = 0 in v² = u² + 2as; (c) the braking distances are 10, 40, 90 m (dry) and 20, 80, 180 m (wet); (d) totals are 20, 60, 120 m for the dry road; (e) learners can state that the braking distance is 4 times as much when the speed doubles. Use a thumbs up/sideways/down check: "Can you get the braking distance at 20 m/s on your own?" Pair a learner who is struggling with one who has completed the table.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Part A (10 min): Whole-class discussion. Learners compare the results with their predictions and explain in their own words, using evidence from the table: (1) why the total stopping distance is more than double when the speed doubles (20 m to 60 m); (2) why the wet road doubles the braking distance (a = -2.5 instead of -5); (3) what happens at 108 km/h on a wet road (30 m reaction + 180 m braking = 210 m). Learners write a claim-evidence-reasoning statement: "Braking distance depends on the square of speed because v² = u² + 2as gives s = u²/2|a|; doubling u multiplies s by 4." Part B (10 min): Link to the phenomenon and slopes. In groups, learners compare the cart (no brakes; it reaches 20 m/s after 100 m) with a matatu stopping from 20 m/s (60 m total on a dry road). They discuss: Why are the signs on the Kinangop descent (steep gradient, slow down, use low gear, runaway truck ramps) there? How does the slope make a long descent dangerous, based on what they learned in Lesson 5 about speed and gravity? What do NTSA rules (speed limits, keeping a safe following distance, no overloading) do to reduce the risk? Part C (5 min): Learners are given the research task for Lessons 6-7 (in groups of 4): the SGR train (scheduling and acceleration), pole vault (motion up and down under g) or construction safety (falling objects). Each group picks one and starts planning how to find and present one linear-motion idea with at least one calculation.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at your predictions from the start of the lesson. Turn to your partner and tell them one thing that was different from what you expected." Cold-call 4 pairs. Ask: "Why does the braking distance grow so much faster than the speed?" WAIT TIME 15 seconds. If needed, point to the equation and ask: "In v² = u² + 2as, the u is squared. If u doubles, what happens to u²?" Then ask: "Mzee Kamau's cart reached 20 m/s with no brakes. A matatu going 72 km/h on a dry road needs 60 m to stop. If a driver is at 108 km/h on a wet road, how far is that? Would a boda-boda rider like Otieno be able to stop?" Cold-call 3 learners. Introduce the Kinangop descent: "Why do you think the signs say 'slow down' at the top of the hill, not halfway down?" Link to Lesson 5 (the danger of speed building up on slopes): the speed gained on a slope is gained as the vehicle descends, and brakes then have to remove much more energy. Say: "What do NTSA rules do about these three ideas: reaction time, speed and road conditions?" Take responses from 4 groups. State the key points clearly and have the class say them: "Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance. Braking distance goes with the square of the speed." Do not re-teach the equations, only apply them. Be sensitive to learners affected by road crashes. Give the research task with a simple rubric: one linear-motion idea, one calculation, one safety or practical message, 3 minutes to present in Lesson 7. Allow digital devices or print media in school.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with phenomenon linking. Learners state a claim (braking distance goes with v²), cite evidence from their table, and give a scientific reason from the equation. Connecting this back to the cart and to Kinangop shows the same physics at work in a new context, which helps learners transfer ideas. The group research task extends the idea to other contexts.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) learners state that stopping distance is the sum of reaction and braking distance; (b) they explain, with numbers, that doubling the speed multiplies the braking distance by 4 and tripling it by 9; (c) they give a link between slope, speed and danger; (d) they name at least two NTSA-related safety measures with a physics reason; (e) each group chooses a research topic with a stated linear-motion idea. Use the CER sentences as an exit check: collect 5 samples and check that the evidence cites actual values from the table.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners revisit the Driving Question Board. Each group reads the question cards on the board and sorts them into: answered by evidence in Lessons 1 to 6, partly answered, not yet answered. For the questions that are answered (for example 'Why does the cart keep getting faster?' and 'How far will it go before it crashes?'), they add an answer card with the evidence and the equation used. They also write new question cards raised today, such as 'Why do heavy lorries need longer to stop?', 'How does a runaway truck ramp work?' or 'What would the cart's stopping distance be if the driver braked?' and add them to the board. Learners tag cards that connect to road safety with a coloured dot.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Come to the board. Take two minutes in your group to read the cards. Which of them can we now answer using stopping distance?" WAIT TIME 10 seconds before they move. Cold-call 3 groups to move a card and justify it by citing evidence ("We moved it because the table showed..."). Ask: "What new questions did today raise? Write one on a new card." Collect at least 4 new cards and read 2 aloud. Point to the learners' question about heavy loads and say: "That is a great question. The cart was 300 kg and its acceleration did not depend on mass. We need to think about whether braking is different." Mark it for Lesson 7 or 8 discussion. Link the key inquiry questions: "How is free fall and speed important in real life? How can the dangers be reduced? Which cards on the board show that?"
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question tracking on the Driving Question Board. Sorting and moving cards makes the growth of class understanding visible and keeps learning tied to the anchoring phenomenon. Writing new questions encourages learners to see science as an ongoing investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) groups move cards to 'answered' only with a stated piece of evidence; (b) at least 4 new, relevant questions are added; (c) some new questions are about road safety or about applying the equations (not only recall). Note learners who contribute to the sorting and those who do not and invite them to speak.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners revise the class model for the mkokoteni (an annotated diagram of the escarpment road with the lorry at the bottom, plus a velocity-time sketch). They add a new section, 'What if it needed to stop?' showing: (a) the cart reaching 20 m/s at 100 m; (b) a matatu stopping from 20 m/s: 20 m reaction, 40 m braking, total 60 m on a dry road, and 80 m braking on a wet road; (c) a note saying 'braking distance goes with the square of the speed' and the equation s = u²/2|a|. In their notebooks, each learner writes a short answer: 'How can we use mathematics to predict how far a vehicle will travel before it stops, and how does that help us to stay safe?' They add a line linking it to the cart: 'The cart has no reaction time and no brakes, so it travels the full 100 m and hits the lorry at 20 m/s (72 km/h).'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Take out your model from Lesson 5. What do we need to add so that it can explain stopping, not only speeding up?" WAIT TIME 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners for ideas. Guide them to add the stopping section and check that the numbers match the table (20 m, 40 m, 60 m total for 20 m/s on dry road; 80 m braking on wet road). Say: "Write one sentence that someone from the Kinangop community could understand: why must a driver slow down early on a steep descent?" Collect 3 sentences and read them out. Remind learners that the full velocity-time graph will be drawn in Lesson 7. Point out to the whole class: "Today we moved from predicting how fast to predicting how far to stop. That is the mathematics that keeps people safe." Collect notebooks or exit slips with the sentence for review.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision. Adding a stopping component to the class model shows learners that the same equations answer a new question, which consolidates the equations and strengthens the link between the phenomenon and real-life safety decisions. Writing for a community audience encourages clear scientific communication.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) the model includes correct numbers (20 m, 40 m, 60 m) and the v² relationship; (b) the written sentence links speed, braking distance and safe driving; (c) the learner mentions that the cart has no brakes or reaction time. Exit-slip check: 'If a matatu's speed goes from 20 m/s to 30 m/s, by what factor does the braking distance increase?' (Expected: 2.25 times, from 40 m to 90 m.) Note who gets it right and who needs support.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners hold the misconception that stopping distance is proportional to speed, and did the table change their minds? Which learners could not tell reaction distance from braking distance? Were learners confident in using v = 0 and a = -5 m/s² in v² = u² + 2as, as practised in Lesson 3? Did the link between Kinangop and the slope make sense after Lesson 5? Was the road-crash discussion handled sensitively? Did every group choose a research topic (SGR train, pole vault or construction safety) with a clear linear-motion idea and a calculation? Which resources (devices or print) were available, and do some groups need printed support for Lesson 7? What would you change next time (for example, more time on the wet road or an extra practice problem)?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that a matatu on Mombasa Road needs a longer total stopping distance as speed rises: on a dry road 20 m at 10 m/s (36 km/h), 60 m at 20 m/s (72 km/h) and 120 m at 30 m/s (108 km/h). The braking distances (10 m, 40 m, 90 m dry; 20 m, 80 m, 180 m wet) grew much faster than the speed.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance. Reaction distance is speed x reaction time (1.0 s), while braking distance comes from v² = u² + 2as with v = 0, which gives u²/2|a|. So doubling the speed multiplies braking distance by 4 and tripling it multiplies it by 9, and a wet road (a = 2.5 m/s²) doubles the braking distance.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that the runaway mkokoteni reaches 20 m/s (72 km/h) with no brakes and hits the lorry, while a matatu travelling at the same speed on a dry road needs 60 m to stop. Because braking distance depends on the square of speed, steep roads such as the Kinangop descent need warning signs and slow, early braking, and NTSA rules on speed and safe distance save lives. The same equations of linear motion that predict the cart's speed and distance also predict how far a vehicle needs to stop.

LESSONS.title: Group Presentations and Building the Class Model: The Mkokoteni's Velocity-Time Graph
LESSONS.aresKeywords: velocity-time graph, gradient, area under graph, acceleration, displacement, mkokoteni, explanatory model, free fall, stopping distance, road safety, NTSA, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: To help learners present their group research on real-life applications of linear motion (SGR train, pole vault, construction safety) and to represent the runaway mkokoteni's motion as a velocity-time graph (gradient = acceleration, area = displacement), linking all concepts from Lessons 1-6 into one class explanatory model.
slo.knowledge: Learners explain terms used in linear motion (distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration). Learners calculate variables of motion using the equations of linear motion with constant acceleration: (1) v = u + at; (2) s = ut + ½at²; (3) v² = u² + 2as; (4) s = ½(u+v)t. Learners investigate the effect of gravity on bodies under free fall. Learners appreciate the significance of linear motion and free fall in real life. For the cart: the v-t graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient 2 m/s², the area under it from 0 to 10 s is 1/2 x 10 x 20 = 100 m, and the s-t graph is a curve (s = t²).
slo.skills: Plotting and reading a velocity-time graph from the mkokoteni table; calculating gradient and area under a graph; communicating research findings in a 3-minute presentation; constructing, using and revising a model (NGSS Developing and Using Models); constructing explanations from evidence (NGSS Constructing Explanations); using mathematics and computational thinking (NGSS); engaging in argument from evidence during cold-call follow-up questions.
slo.attitudes: Communication and collaboration: learners work with peers to discuss and present in plenary the application of linear motion in real life. Learning to learn: learners present findings from assignments in a group discussion. Peace: learners display tolerance and calmness when discussing the application of linear motion in real life. Unity: learners display cooperation and collaboration with others while building the class model. PCI Road safety: increased awareness on how to minimise fatal injuries resulting from road crashes on sloping roads using the concept of free fall of objects.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How is free fall motion important in real life? 2. How can the dangers of free fall in our day-to-day life be mitigated?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 7 pulls together the evidence from Lessons 1-6. Learners have the definitions (L1), the four equations (L2), multi-step problem solving and sign conventions (L3), g from measurement (L4), free fall and why the slope reduces the cart's acceleration to 0.2 of g (L5), and stopping distances and road safety (L6). Here they present their research and add one new idea: the velocity-time graph, where the gradient shows acceleration and the area shows displacement. They use it to build one model that answers the driving question: why the mkokoteni keeps getting faster and how we can predict its speed and distance before the crash. Lesson 8 then consolidates individually.
slo.safetyNotes: No physical drops or moving carts are used in this lesson. Keep aisles clear when groups move to the model wall. Learners handle rulers and pencils only. Presenters should not stand on chairs to reach the model wall. If any group demonstrates a pole vault or similar action, it must be described or shown on paper only, not performed in the classroom.

LESSONS.overview: Mzee Kamau's loaded mkokoteni (300 kg) rolled 100 m down the Limuru-Nairobi escarpment road and hit a parked lorry at 20 m/s (72 km/h). Achieng said, 'It started slowly then flew.' In this double lesson, learners first predict what a graph of the cart's velocity against time would look like and what its area might mean. They then observe three 3-minute group presentations (SGR train, pole vault, construction safety), with the teacher cold-calling 2 members per group for follow-up questions. Next they plot the full mkokoteni table, find the gradient (2 m/s²) and the area (100 m at 10 s), and compare the s-t curve (s = t²). Finally they review the Driving Question Board and build a class explanatory model (annotated diagram plus velocity-time graph) linking motion terms, equations, free fall, gravity and road safety back to the cart.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners recall the video of the runaway mkokoteni and Achieng's words, 'It started slowly then flew.' Individually, then in pairs, they sketch on scrap paper what the graph of the cart's velocity (vertical axis) against time (horizontal axis) might look like for the 10 s down the escarpment, and write one sentence on what the steepness of the line would tell us. They also predict: 'If the cart travelled 100 m in 10 s and finished at 20 m/s, can we find the 100 m from the graph?' Learners write a prediction with a reason. They share in pairs and then hold up sketches.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the question: 'Draw velocity against time for Mzee Kamau's cart from the moment it is released until it hits the lorry.' Say: 'Remember, the cart has no engine and nobody is pushing. Think about what you know from Lessons 1 to 6. Do not use your notes. I want your honest prediction.' WAIT TIME 15 seconds in silence before pairs talk. Walk round and note sketches: straight line through origin, curve, flat line, line that starts high. Cold-call 3 learners with different sketches: 'Why did you draw it that way?' Do not correct. Record sketch types on the board with tally marks. Say: 'Hold on to your sketch. By the end of today we will test it against the evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Predict step) with a Gallery of Initial Ideas: making sketches public and tallied surfaces misconceptions (for example, a curve for velocity, or a flat line because the cart is not pushed) so that they can be tested against the table later. Learners' own ideas become the comparison point for later revision.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe and tally: (a) how many sketches show a rising line (consistent with Lesson 1's claim that velocity keeps increasing), (b) how many start at zero, (c) how many show a straight line versus a curve, (d) how many link the steepness to acceleration. Look for the misconception 'the graph shows the path of the road' (a hill shape). Record the tally on the board for comparison at the end of the lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Part A: Group presentations (3 groups x 3 minutes, plus 1-2 minutes of follow-up each). Groups present their Lesson 6 research on the SGR train, pole vault, and construction safety, each linking to the equations of linear motion, free fall or stopping distance. Listening learners complete a 3-column note sheet: 'Linear motion idea / Equation or term used / Link to the mkokoteni'. After each presentation, the 2 cold-called members answer follow-up questions. Part B: Data to graph. Using the full mkokoteni table (t = 0 to 10 s, v = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20 m/s at t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10 s; s = 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 64, 100 m), learners plot a v-t graph on graph paper (time on x-axis 1 cm = 1 s; velocity on y-axis 1 cm = 2 m/s) and draw the best-fit line. They find the gradient using the points (0, 0) and (10, 20): gradient = 20/10 = 2 m/s², and compare with a = 2.0 m/s² from Lesson 1. Then they find the area of the triangle under the line from 0 to 10 s: 1/2 x 10 x 20 = 100 m, and compare with the table value s = 100 m.
framework.teacherMoves: Before presentations say: 'Presenters have exactly 3 minutes. Audience, your job is to find the link to Mzee Kamau's cart.' Keep time visibly. After each group, cold-call 2 members: 'Member A, which equation of linear motion did your group use and why?' 'Member B, how would your topic change if the road were wet?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds before each answer. If the first answer is incomplete, ask 'What would your partner add?' For the SGR train group ask: 'When the train brakes, is acceleration positive or negative? Why?' For the pole vault group ask: 'At the top of the vault, what is the vertical velocity? What is a?' For the construction safety group ask: 'If a brick falls 20 m from a scaffold, how long does it take and how fast is it moving? (2 s, 20 m/s) How does that compare with the cart?' For Part B say: 'Plot every point. Use a ruler. Then I want you to tell me what the line is doing.' Circulate and ask: 'What is the gradient of your line? What are the units? What does it mean physically?' and 'How could you find the 100 m without using s = t²?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners for the gradient and 3 for the area.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence gathering through peer presentation and data representation (Analysing and Interpreting Data). Presentations broaden the evidence base from the cart to other real-world cases, while plotting the table converts numbers into a visual pattern. Using a graph to see that constant acceleration gives a straight line and that area equals distance builds the mathematical link between the table, the equations and the cart's motion.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check note sheets: each learner should have at least 2 links to the cart per presentation. Observe whether the cold-called members state the correct equation and sign convention (a negative for braking; up positive for the vaulter). Check graphs: points plotted accurately to half a square, straight line through the origin, gradient calculated as 2 m/s² with correct units, area as 100 m with working shown. Listen for the common error of reading the gradient as 20 m/s (the final velocity) or as 10 m/s. Note learners who recognise that the area of 100 m matches the crash distance.

framework.learnerExperience: (20 min) In groups of 4, learners use the graph to explain the cart's motion and answer: (1) Why is the line straight? (constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s², because gravity pulls it down the slope all the time: a = g x 0.2 = 10 x 0.2) (2) Why did Achieng say 'It started slowly then flew'? (velocity starts at 0 and rises 2 m/s every second; distance grows as t²: 25 m by 5 s but 100 m by 10 s). (3) Use the graph to find the cart's velocity at 5 s (10 m/s) and the distance by 5 s as the area of a triangle (1/2 x 5 x 10 = 25 m). (4) Why is the average speed 10 m/s, and where is that seen on the graph? (halfway up the line: (0 + 20)/2). (5) Sketch the s-t graph and explain why it is a curve (s = t²). (6) Compare with the free fall of 20 m: a graph with a gradient of 10 m/s² would reach 20 m/s in 2 s, five times as steep. (7) Using the L6 table link, explain on a sentence strip why doubling speed means 4 times the braking distance, using the idea that the area under a braking v-t graph is displacement. Each group writes a 3-sentence explanation answering 'Why does the cart keep getting faster, and how can we predict how fast and how far?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use only evidence from your graph, the table and Lessons 1 to 6. I want a claim, evidence and reasoning.' Ask: 'The cart has a mass of 300 kg. If it carried 600 kg, would the gradient change? Why or why not?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds. (No: a = g x 0.2 = 2.0 m/s², mass does not change it.) Challenge: 'Someone says the cart is in free fall. Agree or disagree?' Cold-call 3 groups, one member each, using the stem 'I disagree because the acceleration is ___ not ___.' Address the misconception that a straight v-t line means constant velocity: 'Is this line flat? What does flat mean? What does sloping mean?' Prompt reasoning: 'How is the steepness of the free fall line different from the cart line, and what does that tell us about the slope?' Ask 2 members from every group to read their 3-sentence explanation aloud and have the class give a thumbs-up or thumbs-down signal for evidence use.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Think-Pair-Share (Constructing Explanations). Learners use the graph's gradient and area as evidence for causal reasoning: gravity along the slope gives constant acceleration, so the line is straight. Contrasting the cart with free fall (same final speed of 20 m/s, 10 s versus 2 s) sharpens the idea that the slope reduces acceleration to 0.2 of g.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for explanations that include (a) constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s² caused by gravity along the slope, (b) gradient meaning acceleration, (c) area meaning displacement, and (d) why it feels sudden (s grows as t²). Indicators of mastery: correctly states v = 10 m/s and s = 25 m at 5 s from the graph and checks them with v = u + at and s = ½at²; states that mass does not change a; says the cart is not free fall. Misconceptions to note: using a = 10 for the cart; confusing the gradient with the area; saying heavier objects accelerate faster.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners return to the DQB started in Lesson 1. In groups, each takes 3-4 question cards and decides whether each is Answered, Partly answered, or Still open, giving the lesson evidence that supports the decision (for example, 'Why does the cart get faster if nobody pushes it?' answered by L1 and the gradient of 2 m/s²; 'Can we predict how fast it will be?' answered by L2 equations and the table: v = 20 m/s at 10 s; 'Why can't we stop in time on a slope?' answered by L6, with braking distance proportional to v²). Learners move answered cards to the 'Answered' column with a sticky-note evidence statement and write any new questions (for example, 'What happens when friction is included?' or 'How do runaway-truck ramps on the Kinangop road work?') on new cards for Lesson 8 or further study.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Read each question on the board aloud. Can we answer it using evidence from our lessons? Show me the evidence.' WAIT TIME 10 seconds before a group moves a card. Cold-call 4 learners from different groups: 'Which lesson gave you the evidence for that answer?' Push for specifics: 'Give me a number from the table.' Highlight questions that remain open: friction, air resistance and drag, and the real escarpment road. Respond to new questions: 'Great question, we ignored friction in our model. Add it to the Open column.' Link to KICD key inquiry question 2: 'How can the dangers of free fall in our day-to-day life be mitigated?' and point to the NTSA rules and the Kinangop warning signs from Lesson 6.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question tracking on the Driving Question Board (Asking Questions): returning to the learners' own questions shows what the evidence has resolved and what has not, building ownership of the learning and showing that science progresses by refining questions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each card moved to 'Answered' has a correct evidence statement with a number or a named lesson. Listen for the three limits learners should recognise: the model ignores friction and air resistance, the cart is not free fall, and the numbers hold only for the steady 100 m straight section. Note the quality of new questions: those that refer to variables (slope angle, friction, mass, wet road) show deeper understanding.

framework.learnerExperience: (15 min) The class builds one explanatory model on a large sheet on the wall: (1) a side-view diagram of the Limuru-Nairobi escarpment road with the mkokoteni at the top (u = 0), the lorry at the bottom 100 m along the road (20 m vertical drop), and the slope with sin(angle) = 0.2 labelled; (2) arrows for the pull of gravity along the slope, labelled a = g x 0.2 = 2.0 m/s²; (3) time stamps along the slope with v and s from the table (t = 0, 5, 10 s: 0, 10, 20 m/s; 0, 25, 100 m); (4) the velocity-time graph with gradient 2 m/s² and the shaded area of 100 m, and a small s-t curve; (5) a call-out box for free fall: a vertical drop of 20 m takes 2 s, a = 10 m/s², final v = 20 m/s; (6) a call-out box for road safety: stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance, doubling speed multiplies braking distance by 4, with NTSA rules and warning signs like those on the Kinangop descent. Each group adds one labelled component, and the class agrees on the wording. Learners then compare with their initial predictions from the Predict Phase and revise their own sketches in a different colour.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must answer the driving question: why does the cart keep getting faster, and how can we predict how fast and how far? Every part of the model must connect to another part with an arrow and a reason.' Assign components to groups: Group 1 diagram and slope; Group 2 forces and acceleration; Group 3 v-t graph; Group 4 s-t curve and table; Group 5 free fall comparison; Group 6 road safety. WAIT TIME 15 seconds before each group adds its piece, and ask the class, 'Does this match our evidence? Raise a hand if you disagree.' Cold-call 3 learners to trace a path through the model: 'Start at gravity and end at the crash. Tell me the story using the model.' Ask: 'What does the model not yet explain?' (friction, air resistance, the real road). Close by returning to the prediction tally: 'How many of you changed your sketch? What evidence changed your mind?' Preview Lesson 8: 'Next lesson you will explain the cart on your own, so keep this model in mind.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Collaborative Model Building and Revision (Developing and Using Models): the model integrates the motion terms, the equations, graphs, gravity, free fall and safety into one coherent account. Revising the initial sketch makes learning visible and shows that models are improved by evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a checklist: model includes a labelled slope with sin(angle) = 0.2, a = 2.0 m/s² (not 10), table values (v = 20 m/s, s = 100 m at 10 s), the straight v-t line with gradient 2 m/s² and area 100 m, the curved s-t graph, the free fall comparison (2 s versus 10 s, both 20 m/s), and the road safety link. Observe whether learners can trace a causal chain: gravity along the slope, then constant acceleration, then velocity rising 2 m/s every second, then distance growing as t², then a crash at 72 km/h. Check that revised sketches show clear changes with a written reason.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Could every learner explain, in their own words, why the v-t line for the cart is straight and what its gradient and area mean? (2) Which group presentation best connected its topic to the cart, and which needed more help to link the equations of linear motion to their example? (3) Did any learners still use a = 10 m/s² for the cart or call it free fall, and which question exposed it? (4) Were the 3-minute limits and cold-calls managed fairly, so quieter learners spoke? (5) Did the model-building phase allow every learner to contribute? (6) Which DQB questions remain open, and what should Lesson 8 emphasise for the individual written explanation? Note learners who need support with graph plotting, reading the area as a triangle, or unit conversion (km/h divided by 3.6 gives m/s) before Lesson 8.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe about the mkokoteni's motion from the table and graph? (For example: velocity rises by 2 m/s every second, giving a straight line through the origin on the v-t graph; distance grows as t², with s = 25 m at 5 s but 100 m at 10 s; the cart hits the lorry at 20 m/s, or 72 km/h.) What did you observe in the group presentations about linear motion in real life?
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we learn today? (For example: the gradient of a velocity-time graph is acceleration (2 m/s²); the area under it is displacement (1/2 x 10 x 20 = 100 m); a constant acceleration gives a straight line; the s-t graph is a curve; free fall is the same physics with a = g = 10 m/s²; stopping distance rises sharply with speed.)
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How do we now explain the driving question? (For example: gravity pulls the mkokoteni down the slope all the time, giving a constant acceleration of a = g x 0.2 = 2.0 m/s², so its velocity keeps rising from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s; it starts slowly because it starts from rest and feels sudden because distance grows as t²; the equations of linear motion and the v-t graph let us predict speed and distance at any moment, and they show why higher speeds need much longer stopping distances.)

LESSONS.title: Consolidation, DQB Review and Final Explanation: Why the Mkokoteni Keeps Getting Faster and How We Predict It
LESSONS.aresKeywords: final explanation, consolidation, DQB review, constant acceleration, equations of linear motion, free fall, mkokoteni, gravity, velocity-time graph, model comparison

slo.purpose: To consolidate learning from Lessons 1-7 through individual problem solving and a written Final Explanation of the mkokoteni phenomenon, to close the Driving Question Board, and to reflect on how thinking has changed since Lesson 1. No new content is taught.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: a) explain terms used in linear motion (distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration) b) calculate variables of motion using equations of linear motion with constant acceleration c) investigate the effect of gravity on bodies under free fall d) appreciate the significance of linear motion and free fall in real life. Content used: the mkokoteni table (t=10 s, v=20 m/s=72 km/h, s=100 m, a=2.0 m/s²), the free fall comparison (20 m drop: 2 s and 20 m/s in free fall versus 10 s and 20 m/s for the cart), the mango falling from a 5 m branch (t=1 s, v=10 m/s), and a sprinter problem.
slo.skills: Selecting an equation by listing knowns and unknown; applying the sign convention; using the equations with u=0; interpreting the velocity-time graph (gradient = acceleration, area = displacement); constructing a written scientific explanation (claim, evidence, reasoning); comparing an early model with a final model; reflecting in a journal. NGSS practices: Constructing Explanations, Developing and Using Models, Analyzing and Interpreting Data, Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking, Engaging in Argument from Evidence.
slo.attitudes: Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving (solving the structured problem set); Learning to learn (reflecting on how own thinking changed); Communication and collaboration (the whole-class DQB review). Values: Peace (tolerance and calmness when discussing different answers); Unity (cooperation during the DQB review). PCIs: Road safety (minimising fatal injuries from crashes on sloping roads); Life Skills Education (self-awareness through honest reflection on own learning).
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How is free fall motion important in real life? 2. How can the dangers of free fall in our day-to-day life be mitigated?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson of the storyline. Learners pull together everything from Lessons 1-7 to answer the Driving Question: why the runaway mkokoteni on the Limuru escarpment keeps getting faster, and how mathematics predicts exactly how fast and how far it travels before it crashes. It builds on the Lesson 7 class model (annotated diagram plus velocity-time graph) and the DQB, and it shows how far thinking has moved from the Lesson 1 predictions.
slo.safetyNotes: This is a paper-and-discussion lesson, so there are no hazardous activities. Keep the classroom clear of bags while learners move to the DQB. Do not allow learners to test falling objects from desks or windows. Remind learners that the road-safety discussion is about Mzee Kamau's cart, and be sensitive: no one was hurt, but the cart was destroyed.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by revisiting their Lesson 1 predictions about Mzee Kamau's runaway mkokoteni and make a brief new prediction about a new situation, a sprinter starting from rest. They then work individually through a structured problem set set in the anchoring phenomenon and its supporting phenomena: the full mkokoteni table (a=2.0 m/s², v=20 m/s and s=100 m at t=10 s), the free fall comparison (a 20 m vertical drop takes 2 s and gives 20 m/s, but the cart needs 10 s to reach the same 20 m/s because the slope provides only 0.2 of g), the mango falling from a 5 m branch, and a Rift Valley sprinter built like the Lesson 3 runner problem. In the Explain phase learners write an individual Final Explanation (claim, evidence, reasoning) answering the Driving Question. The class then completes the DQB: each remaining question is discussed and answered collectively, with the evidence cited. Finally, learners compare a Lesson 1 model with a final model and write a journal reflection. Achieng's words, 'it started slowly then flew', are used as a thread to check whether learners can now explain what she saw.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their Lesson 1 journals and read their original prediction about why Mzee Kamau's 300 kg mkokoteni kept getting faster. In pairs (2 minutes) they underline any idea they now think was incomplete. Then each learner writes a quick prediction (individually, 3 minutes) for a NEW case: a Rift Valley 400 m runner starts from rest and accelerates at 4 m/s² for 2.5 s. They predict whether she will be running faster than 5 m/s, 10 m/s or 20 m/s, and roughly how far she will have gone. They also predict: if the cart were dropped straight down a 20 m vertical drop instead of rolling down the slope, would it reach the bottom faster or slower than 10 s, and would its final speed be greater, smaller or the same as 20 m/s?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your journals to Lesson 1. Read what you wrote about why the cart kept getting faster. Does it still make sense to you?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds in silence. Cold-call 3 learners: 'What did you write in Lesson 1?' Do not correct them yet. Then say: 'Today you are the experts. Before we calculate, predict: the runner starts from rest and accelerates at 4 m/s² for 2.5 s. Is her speed after 2.5 s closer to 5, 10 or 20 m/s?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Ask all learners to show 1, 2 or 3 fingers for their choice, and record the tally on the board. Then ask: 'If the cart fell straight down a 20 m drop, faster or slower than 10 s?' Cold-call 2 learners to give reasons. Record predictions and say: 'We will check these against the evidence by the end of the lesson.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with Revisiting of Prior Ideas: learners confront their own earlier thinking and commit to new predictions before calculating. Committing to a prediction makes a later correct calculation more memorable, and it exposes any remaining misconceptions (for example, that heavier carts accelerate faster or that speed must come from a continuing push).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners (a) can locate and read their Lesson 1 prediction, (b) justify their runner prediction using the idea of acceleration as change in velocity per second rather than a vague 'she is fast', and (c) mention gravity or the slope in the cart prediction. Tally the finger votes and note the 3 most common misconceptions on the side board: 'a force is needed to keep moving', 'mass changes the acceleration', 'a steeper path gives a different final speed'. Use the tally to decide which problems to prioritise during circulation.

framework.learnerExperience: Individually, learners complete the structured 'Mkokoteni Problem Set' (about 25 minutes) in their exercise books, using g = 10 m/s² and the sign convention. They must list the knowns (u, v, a, s, t), name the unknown, choose the equation, and show units. Part A (the cart, a=2.0 m/s², u=0): (1) Use v = u + at to find the cart's velocity at t = 2 s and t = 5 s (4 m/s, 10 m/s). (2) Use s = ut + ½at² to find its distance at t = 5 s and t = 10 s (25 m, 100 m). (3) Use v² = u² + 2as to check the speed after 100 m (v² = 400, so v = 20 m/s) and convert to km/h (72 km/h). (4) Use s = ½(u+v)t to confirm the average speed over 10 s (10 m/s). Part B (supporting phenomena): (5) The mango falls from a 5 m branch of a mango tree in a school compound with u=0 and a=g: find t and v (1 s, 10 m/s). (6) Free fall comparison: find the time and speed for a 20 m vertical drop (2 s, 20 m/s) and explain why the cart needs 10 s to reach the same 20 m/s. (7) The Rift Valley 400 m runner starts from rest and accelerates at 4 m/s² for 2.5 s: find v and s (10 m/s, 12.5 m). Part C (graph): (8) Sketch the cart's velocity-time graph for 0-10 s, mark the gradient (2 m/s²) and calculate the area (½ x 10 x 20 = 100 m). Learners who finish early attempt a challenge: at what time is the cart exactly half-way (50 m) down the slope? (t = sqrt(50) which is about 7.1 s, and v is about 14 m/s). Learners who need support use the quick-reference card of the four equations (v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u+v)t) and the 'list knowns, find the unknown' organiser from Lesson 2.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'This is your chance to show what YOU can do, not what your group can do. Silent, independent work for the first 20 minutes.' Circulate with a clipboard and check the first line of each learner's working: 'Show me your list of knowns. Which one is missing?' Do not give answers; use prompts such as 'What is u for a cart released from rest?' and 'Why is a = 2 and not 10 for the cart?' For learners making the error of using a = 10 for the cart, ask: 'Is the cart in free fall? What fraction of g does the slope give?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after every prompt before saying anything else. After 20 minutes allow learners to compare final answers in pairs for 5 minutes only. Stop at 25 minutes and cold-call 4 different learners to state one answer each (cart at 5 s, mango, runner, graph area) and ask the class to give a thumbs up/down for agreement. Do not collect marks yet; the answers become evidence for the Explain phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Individual Problem Solving with Structured Data (Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking): working through the same cart data in several equation forms shows that one idea, constant acceleration, produces consistent predictions (the answers v = 20 m/s and s = 100 m agree whichever equation is used). Comparing the 2 s free fall with the 10 s cart descent makes the role of the slope visible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each learner: (a) lists knowns and the unknown before calculating; (b) uses a = 2.0 m/s² for the cart and a = 10 m/s² only for the mango and the vertical drop; (c) reports units and the correct sign; (d) gets v = 20 m/s and s = 100 m for the cart at t = 10 s; (e) gets 10 m/s and 12.5 m for the runner; (f) draws a straight line through the origin for the velocity-time graph with gradient 2 m/s². Tick on a class checklist: 'Selects correct equation', 'Correct a', 'Correct units', 'Graph correct'. Learners with fewer than 5 of 8 correct are flagged for a short follow-up conversation.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners write the Final Explanation individually (about 15 minutes) in answer to the Driving Question: 'Why does a runaway mkokoteni on the Limuru escarpment keep getting faster, and how can we use mathematics to predict exactly how fast and how far it will travel before it crashes?' They use a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning frame: CLAIM: a one-sentence answer. EVIDENCE: at least three numbers from the mkokoteni table (for example 4 m/s at 2 s, 10 m/s at 5 s and 25 m, 20 m/s (72 km/h) and 100 m at 10 s), plus the free fall comparison. REASONING: link the evidence to the science: gravity pulls the cart down the slope all the time; this gives a constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s² (g x 0.2) so velocity rises by 2 m/s every second; it starts slowly because velocity begins at zero; it feels sudden because s = t², so 25 m by 5 s but 100 m by 10 s; the equations of linear motion predict speed and distance at any moment; free fall is the same physics with a = g = 10 m/s² on a vertical path; the cart takes 10 s for the same 20 m/s that free fall reaches in 2 s because the slope provides only 0.2 of g. They must also explain Achieng's statement, 'it started slowly then flew'. Learners include a labelled sketch with the velocity-time graph. In the last 3 minutes they swap with a partner, who uses a checklist to say whether the explanation includes gravity, constant acceleration, the equations, and the free fall comparison.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Now write the explanation you would give Mzee Kamau if he asked why his cart flew away from him.' Display the CER frame and the checklist on the board (gravity; constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s²; numbers from the table; s = t²; equations; free fall comparison). Remind learners: 'Use the words and numbers from our class model, not just the formula.' Circulate and read over shoulders; ask 'Where in your writing do you explain WHY it keeps getting faster when nobody is pushing?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then let the learner revise. Ask 2 learners with different strengths to read their reasoning aloud; cold-call 3 more to name one piece of evidence they used. Explicitly avoid giving a model answer until the partner check is done. During the partner swap say: 'Tick, do not rewrite. Give your partner one thing that is strong and one thing missing.' Collect the explanations for scoring with the rubric.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (Constructing Explanations): learners must connect numerical evidence to causal mechanisms (gravity gives constant acceleration), which turns calculation into explanation. Peer checking with a shared checklist supports Engaging in Argument from Evidence and lets learners calibrate their own writing against the criteria.
framework.formativeAssessment: Score each Final Explanation 0-3 on four criteria: (1) Cause: identifies gravity acting down the slope all the time (no engine or push needed); (2) Constant acceleration: states 2.0 m/s² and that velocity rises by 2 m/s every second; (3) Evidence: uses at least 3 correct values from the table (v=20 m/s and s=100 m at 10 s) and the free fall comparison; (4) Prediction: states that the equations of linear motion let us calculate speed and distance at any time. Exceeds: all four at level 3 and explains both 'starts slowly' (v begins at 0) and 'feels sudden' (s = t²). Meets: all four at level 2 or higher. Approaches: gravity named but acceleration or numbers incomplete. Below: describes the motion without a cause. Watch for the misconception that the cart's mass makes it accelerate more (acceleration is 2.0 m/s² regardless of mass) and for any use of a = 10 for the cart.

framework.learnerExperience: The class conducts the final DQB review (about 15 minutes). The board has the questions from Lesson 1 and those added during Lessons 2-7 (for example: Why does it start slowly? Does the heavy maize make it faster? Would a steeper road be worse? How is free fall different from the cart? How can the dangers be reduced?). Learners, in rows, each take one question from the board. Individually they write a 1-2 sentence answer on a sticky note with the evidence (lesson and number) and place it next to the question. The class then discusses the questions that remain unanswered or disputed, and answers them collectively. Learners link the final two KICD inquiry questions: (1) How is free fall motion important in real life? (for example, estimating drop heights from impact speed such as the 45 m drop from a 30 m/s impact, the mango tree, pole vault and construction safety); (2) How can the dangers of free fall and fast descent be mitigated? (road signs on the Kinangop descent, NTSA rules, lower speeds because braking distance grows with the square of the speed, safe handling of mkokotenis on slopes, helmets and barriers). Any question that cannot be answered by the lesson content is moved to a 'Future Questions' section for further investigation (for example, the effect of friction and air resistance on the cart).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Stand up and look at our board. Pick one question you can now answer with evidence. Write the answer and the number that supports it.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before learners move. For each question that stays blank, ask: 'Who can answer this using something we measured or calculated?' Cold-call 5 learners to read and defend a note, and use the prompt 'What evidence tells us that?' For disputed answers, invite a second learner to challenge respectfully (Peace and Unity): 'Do you agree, and what number supports you?' Mark each question as 'Answered', 'Partly answered' or 'New question' with different coloured markers. Say: 'Which question did we not fully answer? Why? What would we need to investigate?' to model that science leaves open questions. End by reading the final status aloud: for example 'We have answered all questions about speed and distance; friction and air resistance remain for future study.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Review (Engaging in Argument from Evidence): returning to the learners' own questions shows how far the class's understanding has grown, and requiring evidence for each answer prevents unsupported claims. Recording questions that remain open models how scientific inquiry continues.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) every learner placing an answered note with the supporting evidence, (b) answers that cite specific numbers (for example '20 m/s at 10 s', 'a = g x 0.2 = 2.0 m/s²'), (c) learners who respectfully challenge or add to a peer's answer, (d) reasonable answers to the two KICD inquiry questions that connect free fall and speed to road safety and NTSA rules. Count the questions answered and partly answered and record the percentage for the class record. Note which learners still ask 'why does it keep speeding up?', as this signals a need for one more conversation.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners complete the model comparison and journal reflection (about 15 minutes). Step 1 (5 minutes): in their journals they draw two diagrams side by side. LEFT: their Lesson 1 model/prediction of the cart (copied from the journal). RIGHT: their final model, an annotated diagram of the Limuru-Nairobi slope showing the 100 m of road, the vertical drop of 20 m, the force of gravity pulling the cart down the slope, the constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s², velocity labels at t = 0, 2, 5 and 10 s (0, 4, 10 and 20 m/s), the distance labels (0, 4, 25 and 100 m), the lorry at the bottom, and the velocity-time graph (straight line through the origin, gradient 2 m/s², area 100 m). A small inset shows the free fall comparison (20 m drop: 2 s, 20 m/s). Step 2 (10 minutes): learners write a journal reflection using these starters: 'In Lesson 1 I thought... Now I know... The evidence that changed my mind was... The role of gravity is... The role of constant acceleration is... The equations of linear motion help us because... If I could speak to Mzee Kamau, I would tell him... Something I still wonder about is...' Learners also revisit the opening predictions (runner 10 m/s; cart 20 m drop faster than 10 s and the same 20 m/s) and mark them correct or incorrect with an explanation.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Compare your first model with your final model. What has changed? What stayed the same?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before learners begin writing. Circulate and ask: 'Where in your final model can I see why the speed keeps increasing?' and 'Show me where the model predicts 20 m/s.' Insist on labels with units. Select 3 learners (cold-call) to share one sentence from their reflection beginning 'In Lesson 1 I thought... Now I know...'. Return to the board tally from the Predict phase and ask: 'Which predictions were right? Which changed?' Reveal the answers (runner 10 m/s and 12.5 m; the 20 m vertical drop is faster at 2 s and gives the same 20 m/s) and ask learners to say why. Close with: 'Gravity does not need an engine or a push. A constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s² turns 0 m/s into 72 km/h in just 10 s. That is why we respect steep roads and why NTSA signs matter.' Collect journals for the portfolio.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model Comparison and Reflective Journaling (Developing and Using Models; Learning to Learn): placing the early model next to the final model makes conceptual change visible, and writing about the evidence that changed their minds helps learners to consolidate the causal story (gravity, constant acceleration, equations, free fall) and see themselves as people who can predict real events.
framework.formativeAssessment: Final model checklist: (1) gravity or the slope shown as the cause; (2) acceleration 2.0 m/s² stated with units; (3) at least three correct velocity or distance values from the table; (4) velocity-time graph with gradient 2 m/s² and area 100 m; (5) free fall comparison shown; (6) a clear difference from the Lesson 1 model. Journal indicators: names at least one specific idea that changed, cites evidence, and links to road safety. Exceeds: all six features plus a genuine new question. Meets: at least five features. Approaches: three or four. Below: fewer than three. Record the result in the learner's profile as evidence for Sub-Strand 3.2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) How many learners could explain BOTH 'it started slowly' (velocity begins at zero) AND 'it feels sudden' (distance grows as t²) without prompting? (2) Did any learner still use a = 10 m/s² for the cart or suggest that heavier loads accelerate faster? If so, which activity from Lessons 4-5 should be revisited? (3) Compare the Lesson 1 and final models for 5 learners: what changed most (cause, numbers, graph)? (4) Which DQB questions stayed open, and should they become a future project (for example friction on the escarpment road, SGR braking, pole vault)? (5) Were the conditions for the individual problem set fair, with enough time and a quick-reference card for learners who needed support? (6) How did Peace and Unity show during the DQB review? Record the learners who need extra support on equation selection and plan a short clinic before the end-of-strand assessment.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the mkokoteni released from rest on the Limuru-Nairobi escarpment slope speeds up steadily: 0 m/s at 0 s, 4 m/s at 2 s, 10 m/s at 5 s and 20 m/s (72 km/h) at 10 s after 100 m. We observed that a mango dropped from a 5 m branch reaches 10 m/s after 1 s, and that objects dropped from 2.0 m took about 0.64 s regardless of what they were.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that velocity increases by 2 m/s every second because the cart has a constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s² (g x 0.2), caused by gravity pulling it down the slope all the time. We learned the four equations of linear motion, how to choose the right one by listing knowns and the unknown, and that on a velocity-time graph the gradient is the acceleration and the area is the displacement. We learned that free fall is the same motion with a = g = 10 m/s² on a vertical path.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The mkokoteni keeps getting faster even with no one pushing because gravity acts on it down the slope all the time, giving a constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s². It starts slowly because its velocity begins at 0 m/s, and the crash feels sudden because the distance grows as t² (25 m by 5 s but 100 m by 10 s). Using v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as we can predict that it reaches 20 m/s (72 km/h) after 100 m and 10 s. In a 20 m free fall the same 20 m/s is reached in just 2 s, because the slope gives the cart only 0.2 of g. This is why high speeds need much longer stopping distances and why road-safety rules on steep roads matter.
