FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: General Science Grade 10 – 3.2 Linear Motion: Final Explanation
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: This is your Final Explanation for the Driving Question: Why does a runaway mkokoteni on the Limuru escarpment keep getting faster, and how can we use mathematics to predict exactly how fast and how far it will travel before it crashes? Work on your own. Write your answers in the space under each prompt. Use what you observed, measured and calculated in Lessons 1 to 7. Show every calculation: write the known values with units, name the equation you choose, and give your final answer with units. Use g = 10 m/s² in all calculations. Ignore friction and air resistance unless the question says otherwise. Remember Mzee Kamau's mkokoteni (300 kg when loaded) is released from rest on a straight, steady slope on the Limuru-Nairobi escarpment road where sin(angle) = 0.2. It crashes into a parked lorry after 100 m along the road.

sections.title: Part 1: Explaining what Achieng saw
sections.prompt:
Achieng, a bystander, said: 'It started slowly then flew.' Mzee Kamau's mkokoteni has no engine and nobody was pushing it. Write a Claim, Evidence, Reasoning explanation of why the cart keeps getting faster. In your answer:
(a) State your claim.
(b) Use at least three values from the cart's motion (for example, its speed at different times) as evidence.
(c) Explain why the cart started slowly, and why the crash felt so sudden, using the idea of how distance changes with time.
(d) Say whether the cart's motion is free fall, and explain your answer.
sections.exemplar:
Claim: The mkokoteni keeps getting faster because gravity pulls it down the slope all the time. This gives it a constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s² (a = g × 0.2 = 10 × 0.2), so its velocity increases steadily even though nobody pushes it and it has no engine.

Evidence: Released from rest, the cart's velocity rises by 2 m/s every second. It is 4 m/s after 2 s, 10 m/s after 5 s and 20 m/s (72 km/h) after 10 s, when it has travelled 100 m and hits the lorry. The distance is 25 m by 5 s but 100 m by 10 s.

Reasoning: Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time. Because the force of gravity down the slope acts all the time, the acceleration stays constant and the velocity keeps growing by 2 m/s each second. The cart started slowly because its velocity began at 0 m/s, so it covered only 1 m in the first second. The crash felt sudden because with u = 0 the distance grows as s = t². The cart covers 25 m in the first 5 s but 75 m more in the next 5 s, so the last seconds were very fast. The cart is not in free fall. Free fall has a = g = 10 m/s² on a vertical path. The slope gives the cart only 0.2 of g, so its acceleration is 2 m/s².

Note: Achieng's words 'started slowly then flew' match this. The speed starts at zero and grows every second, and the distance covered in each second grows too.

sections.title: Part 2: Predicting the crash using the equations of linear motion
sections.prompt:
The cart is released from rest (u = 0) with a = 2.0 m/s² and crashes after travelling 100 m along the slope.
(a) List the five variables used in the equations of linear motion and the knowns and the unknown for finding the speed at the crash.
(b) Choose one of the four equations of linear motion, explain in words why it is the right one, and calculate the speed at the crash in m/s and in km/h.
(c) Use a different equation to find the time taken to reach the lorry, and show that it agrees with the data from the lessons.
(d) Find the speed of the cart after it has travelled 25 m. Then compare 25 m with 100 m: by what factor has the distance changed, by what factor has the speed changed, and what does this tell you about how speed depends on distance?
sections.exemplar:
(a) The five variables are u (initial velocity, m/s), v (final velocity, m/s), a (acceleration, m/s²), s (displacement, m) and t (time, s). Knowns: u = 0 m/s, a = 2.0 m/s², s = 100 m. Unknown: v. (t is not given and is not needed.)

(b) The equation that contains u, a, s and v, but not t, is v² = u² + 2as. v² = 0 + 2 × 2.0 × 100 = 400 m²/s², so v = 20 m/s. In km/h: 20 × 3.6 = 72 km/h.

(c) Use v = u + at: 20 = 0 + 2.0 × t, so t = 20 ÷ 2.0 = 10 s. Check with s = ut + ½at²: s = 0 + ½ × 2.0 × 10² = 100 m. This agrees with the crash at 10 s after 100 m.

(d) With s = 25 m: v² = 0 + 2 × 2.0 × 25 = 100, so v = 10 m/s. Going from 25 m to 100 m, the distance becomes four times as large (100 ÷ 25 = 4), while the speed goes from 10 m/s to 20 m/s, which is two times as large. So the speed is not proportional to the distance: the distance must become four times as large for the speed to double (because v² = 2as, v depends on the square root of s).

sections.title: Part 3: Free fall compared with the cart
sections.prompt:
Class drop data: a rubber bung, a stone and a crumpled paper ball were each dropped from h = 2.0 m. The mean times of 5 trials were 0.63 s, 0.64 s and 0.65 s respectively.
(a) What do these results show about the effect of mass on how objects fall when air resistance is negligible?
(b) Use the class mean time of 0.64 s to estimate g, and explain why we use g = 10 m/s² in calculations.
(c) A stone is dropped from rest through a vertical drop of 20 m, the same vertical drop as the cart's. Calculate the time taken and the speed on reaching the ground.
(d) Compare your answers in (c) with the cart's time and speed. Explain the difference in time using the idea of the slope, and say what type of slope free fall represents.
sections.exemplar:
(a) The three objects have very different masses but fell in almost the same time (0.63 s, 0.64 s, 0.65 s), and the small differences are within reaction-time error. So when air resistance is negligible, all objects fall with the same acceleration due to gravity, regardless of mass.

(b) g = 2h/t² (from s = ½at² with u = 0) = 2 × 2.0 ÷ 0.64² = 4 ÷ 0.4096 = 9.8 m/s². We use g = 10 m/s² because it is a convenient value very close to the measured one, and the difference from our result is small enough to be explained by reaction-time error.

(c) Take down as positive, u = 0, a = 10 m/s², s = 20 m. s = ½at², so 20 = ½ × 10 × t², t² = 4, t = 2 s. v = u + at = 0 + 10 × 2 = 20 m/s.

(d) The stone and the cart both reach 20 m/s after a 20 m vertical drop, but the stone takes 2 s while the cart takes 10 s. The slope only provides 0.2 of g, so the cart's acceleration is 2 m/s² instead of 10 m/s², and it takes five times longer to reach the same speed. Free fall is the extreme case of a vertical slope (sin = 1), where a = g.

sections.title: Part 4: Slowing down and the sign convention
sections.prompt:
A boda-boda rider, Otieno, is travelling at 15 m/s and brakes before a police check with a constant acceleration of -3 m/s².
(a) Explain what the negative sign tells you, and compare it with the sign of the cart's acceleration down the slope.
(b) Calculate how long Otieno takes to stop and how far he travels while stopping.
(c) A ball is thrown upward at 15 m/s from a 20 m high Mombasa rooftop. Taking up as positive, state the acceleration of the ball at the top of its path and explain your answer. Then calculate its velocity when it hits the ground.
sections.exemplar:
(a) The negative sign means the acceleration is in the opposite direction to the motion, so the velocity decreases (deceleration). Otieno takes the direction of motion as positive and his acceleration points backwards. The cart's acceleration of +2.0 m/s² is in the same direction as its motion down the slope, so its velocity increases.

(b) u = 15 m/s, v = 0, a = -3 m/s². Time: v = u + at gives 0 = 15 - 3t, so t = 5 s. Distance: v² = u² + 2as gives 0 = 225 + 2(-3)s, so s = 225 ÷ 6 = 37.5 m. Check: s = ½(u+v)t = ½ × 15 × 5 = 37.5 m.

(c) The acceleration of the ball is a = -10 m/s² all the time, including at the top, where v = 0 for an instant. Gravity keeps acting, so the velocity keeps changing by 10 m/s each second downward. The ball ends at the ground, which is 20 m below the start, so s = -20 m. Using v² = u² + 2as: v² = 225 + 2(-10)(-20) = 225 + 400 = 625, so v = -25 m/s (the negative root because it moves downward). The ball hits the ground at 25 m/s downward. Check: it takes 4 s, since v = 15 - 10 × 4 = -25 m/s.

sections.title: Part 5: Road safety and the final explanation
sections.prompt:
A matatu on Mombasa Road has a driver reaction time of 1.0 s. On a dry road, braking gives a deceleration of 5 m/s². On a wet road, the deceleration is 2.5 m/s².
(a) The matatu travels at 72 km/h. Convert this to m/s, then calculate the reaction distance, the braking distance on a dry road and the total stopping distance.
(b) Find the braking distance of the same matatu on a wet road, and compare it with the dry road.
(c) The matatu's speed is increased to 108 km/h. Find the new braking distance on a dry road, and say by what factor it has changed compared with part (a) and why.
(d) Explain how your answers help us understand why the Kinangop descent has warning signs and why a runaway mkokoteni with no brakes is so dangerous. Suggest TWO ways to reduce the dangers of speed on steep roads.
sections.exemplar:
(a) 72 km/h ÷ 3.6 = 20 m/s. Reaction distance = speed × reaction time = 20 × 1.0 = 20 m. Braking distance: v² = u² + 2as with v = 0, so 0 = 400 + 2(-5)s and s = 400 ÷ 10 = 40 m. Total stopping distance = 20 + 40 = 60 m.

(b) Wet road: s = u²/2|a| = 400 ÷ (2 × 2.5) = 400 ÷ 5 = 80 m. The wet-road braking distance is 80 m, which is double the 40 m on a dry road, because the deceleration is half as large.

(c) 108 km/h ÷ 3.6 = 30 m/s. Braking distance = 900 ÷ 10 = 90 m. This is 90 ÷ 40 = 2.25 times the 40 m at 20 m/s. Braking distance depends on the square of speed (u²/2|a|), so increasing the speed by a factor of 1.5 multiplies the braking distance by 1.5² = 2.25. (Doubling the speed multiplies the braking distance by 4, and tripling it multiplies it by 9.)

(d) The mkokoteni reaches 20 m/s (72 km/h) with no brakes, and a matatu at the same speed needs 60 m to stop on a dry road, so a cart that cannot brake cannot avoid the lorry. Because braking distance grows with the square of the speed, steep roads like the Kinangop descent have warning signs so drivers slow down early. Ways to reduce the danger: (1) drive at a lower speed and brake early on slopes, following NTSA speed and safe-distance rules; (2) keep a larger gap from the vehicle ahead and reduce speed on wet roads. (Other valid answers: apply a handbrake or put a block under a cart's wheels when parked on a slope.)

rubric.excellent: Gives a clear claim that gravity acts down the slope all the time giving a constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s². Uses at least three correct cart values (such as 4 m/s at 2 s, 10 m/s at 5 s, 20 m/s at 10 s and 100 m). Explains why it starts slowly and why the crash feels sudden (s = t²), and correctly says the cart is not in free fall.
rubric.proficient: Gives a correct claim with some correct data, and explains acceleration, but explains only one of 'starts slowly' or 'feels sudden', or does not address free fall.
rubric.developing: Claim is unclear or only says the cart is 'pulled' or 'pushed' without linking to constant acceleration, with little or no data used.

rubric.criterion: Using the equations of linear motion
rubric.excellent: Lists the five variables with units, writes the knowns and unknown, chooses a suitable equation and justifies the choice, calculates correctly with units (20 m/s, 72 km/h, 10 s, 10 m/s at 25 m), verifies with a second equation, and correctly compares how distance and speed change between 25 m and 100 m.
rubric.proficient: Chooses suitable equations and gets most answers correct with units, but gives little justification for the choice or does not check with a second equation.
rubric.developing: Equations are chosen at random or substituted incorrectly, or answers have missing or wrong units.

rubric.criterion: Free fall and the comparison with the slope
rubric.excellent: Explains that mass does not change the fall time, estimates g correctly (9.8 m/s²) and explains the use of 10 m/s². Calculates 2 s and 20 m/s for the 20 m drop and explains that the slope gives only 0.2 of g, with free fall as the extreme case of a vertical slope.
rubric.proficient: Calculates the free-fall values correctly and says the cart is slower, but the explanation of why (the slope fraction of g) is incomplete.
rubric.developing: Does not link results to the effect of mass or to the slope, or uses a = 10 m/s² for the cart.

rubric.criterion: Sign convention and use of scalar/vector terms
rubric.excellent: Chooses a positive direction explicitly, interprets negative acceleration as opposite to the motion, correctly uses a = -10 m/s² for the upward-thrown ball including at the top, and gets the 37.5 m, 5 s and -25 m/s answers with correct signs.
rubric.proficient: Uses signs mostly correctly and gets most answers right, but does not explain the signs or makes one sign error.
rubric.developing: Does not use signs consistently, or says the acceleration is zero at the top of the ball's path.

rubric.criterion: Applying the ideas to road safety
rubric.excellent: Converts units correctly, calculates reaction, braking and total stopping distances (20 m, 40 m, 60 m; 80 m wet; 90 m at 30 m/s), explains the square relationship, and gives two sensible ways to reduce danger linked to Kinangop signs and NTSA rules.
rubric.proficient: Calculates most distances correctly and gives sensible safety measures, but explanation of the square relationship is weak.
rubric.developing: Makes errors in unit conversion or stopping distance, or gives safety ideas that are not linked to the calculations.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: Why does a runaway mkokoteni on the Limuru escarpment keep getting faster — and how can we use mathematics to predict exactly how fast and how far it will travel before it crashes?

lessons.title: The Runaway Mkokoteni: Why Does It Keep Getting Faster?
lessons.observed: We watched or studied a runaway mkokoteni (300 kg loaded with maize) released from rest on the Limuru-Nairobi escarpment road. It started slowly, then went much faster, and crashed into a parked lorry after 100 m in about 10 s. The gaps between its positions grew each second, and its average speed was 10 m/s.
lessons.learned: Distance is total path length (scalar, m); displacement is the straight-line change in position with direction (vector, m). Speed is distance/time (scalar); velocity is displacement/time (vector). Acceleration is change in velocity per unit time (m/s²). A 400 m lap has distance 400 m but displacement 0 m. The cart's velocity rises by 2 m/s every second, so it accelerates at 2 m/s².
lessons.explained: The cart has no engine and no one pushing it, yet it keeps getting faster because gravity pulls it down the slope all the time, so its velocity increases steadily from zero. It starts slowly because its velocity begins at zero. We still need mathematics (the equations of linear motion) to predict exactly how fast and how far it travels, which we will build in the next lessons.

lessons.title: Equations of Linear Motion: Choosing the Right Equation
lessons.observed: What did we observe or work out today? (Examples: the matatu on Thika Road reaches v = 12 m/s and s = 48 m after 8 s; the mkokoteni table for t = 1 to 5 s gives v = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 m/s and s = 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 m.)
lessons.learned: What did we learn about the equations of linear motion? (Include the five variables u, v, a, s, t with units, the four equations, and the rule for choosing: list the knowns and the unknown, then pick the equation that has exactly those four variables.)
lessons.explained: How does this help explain the driving question? (Use the cart's constant acceleration of 2 m/s² to explain why the velocity rises by 2 m/s every second, why the cart felt sudden, and how the equations let us predict its speed and distance at any moment.)

lessons.title: Problem Solving with the Equations of Linear Motion: Slowing Down and Going Upward
lessons.observed: We solved the Problem Set. The Rift Valley runner reached 10 m/s after 2.5 s and covered 12.5 m. The boda-boda travelling at 15 m/s with a = -3 m/s² stopped after 5 s and 37.5 m. The ball thrown upward at 15 m/s from the 20 m Mombasa rooftop rose 11.25 m more in 1.5 s (31.25 m above the ground), reached the ground at t = 4 s and hit it at -25 m/s (25 m/s downward).
lessons.learned: We learned to pick a positive direction first, list the knowns with signs, and choose the equation that has the unknown. Slowing down gives a negative a (opposite sign to v). For a ball thrown upward, a = -10 m/s² all the time, even at the top, where v = 0. The same equations work for speeding up, slowing down and vertical motion, just like for Mzee Kamau's mkokoteni (a = +2.0 m/s² down the slope).
lessons.explained: The mkokoteni keeps getting faster because its acceleration is in the same direction as its motion (a = +2.0 m/s² down the slope), so its velocity grows by 2 m/s every second. A braking boda-boda has a negative acceleration because it opposes the motion, so its velocity falls. Because acceleration is constant in each case, the equations of linear motion let us predict speed, distance and time at any moment, and a consistent sign convention is what makes these predictions correct.

lessons.title: Investigating Free Fall: Predict and Observe
lessons.observed: We dropped a rubber bung, a stone and a crumpled paper ball from 2.0 m. Mean fall times were 0.63 s, 0.64 s and 0.65 s (class mean 0.64 s), almost the same although the masses were very different. A flat sheet of paper fell more slowly than the crumpled ball.
lessons.learned: When air resistance is negligible, all objects fall with the same acceleration due to gravity, regardless of mass. Using s = ½at² with u = 0, g = 2h/t² = 4/0.64² = 9.8 m/s², and we use g = 10 m/s² in calculations. Differences are within reaction-time error.
lessons.explained: Gravity pulls on the mkokoteni all the time, so it keeps getting faster, and free fall shows what gravity does on a vertical path: every second adds about 10 m/s to the speed of any object. The cart on the escarpment is not in free fall, so its acceleration is smaller than g (to be investigated in Lesson 5), but the same equations apply to predict its speed and distance.

lessons.title: Freely Falling Bodies: Explain and Calculate
lessons.observed: What did we observe and calculate today? (Include: the mango from the 5 m branch takes t = 1 s and lands at v = 10 m/s; an object hitting the ground at 30 m/s was dropped from 45 m and fell for 3 s; the cart at s = 25 m has v = 10 m/s after t = 5 s; a 20 m free fall takes 2 s and gives 20 m/s while the cart takes 10 s for the same 20 m/s.)
lessons.learned: What did we learn? (Include: with u = 0 and a = g = 10 m/s², the equations of linear motion predict time, speed and height for freely falling bodies; mass does not change the acceleration; the mkokoteni is not in free fall because on the slope its acceleration is g x 0.2 = 2 m/s²; free fall is the extreme case of a vertical slope.)
lessons.explained: How can we now explain the phenomenon? (Include: the cart keeps getting faster because gravity pulls it down the slope all the time, so its velocity rises by 2 m/s every second; it starts slowly because velocity begins at zero and feels sudden because distance grows as t²; the same equations predict 20 m/s (72 km/h) after 10 s and 100 m, and show why steep roads are dangerous.)

lessons.title: Road Safety: Stopping Distance and Real-Life Applications of Linear Motion
lessons.observed: We observed that a matatu on Mombasa Road needs a longer total stopping distance as speed rises: on a dry road 20 m at 10 m/s (36 km/h), 60 m at 20 m/s (72 km/h) and 120 m at 30 m/s (108 km/h). The braking distances (10 m, 40 m, 90 m dry; 20 m, 80 m, 180 m wet) grew much faster than the speed.
lessons.learned: We learned that stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance. Reaction distance is speed x reaction time (1.0 s), while braking distance comes from v² = u² + 2as with v = 0, which gives u²/2|a|. So doubling the speed multiplies braking distance by 4 and tripling it multiplies it by 9, and a wet road (a = 2.5 m/s²) doubles the braking distance.
lessons.explained: We can explain that the runaway mkokoteni reaches 20 m/s (72 km/h) with no brakes and hits the lorry, while a matatu travelling at the same speed on a dry road needs 60 m to stop. Because braking distance depends on the square of speed, steep roads such as the Kinangop descent need warning signs and slow, early braking, and NTSA rules on speed and safe distance save lives. The same equations of linear motion that predict the cart's speed and distance also predict how far a vehicle needs to stop.

lessons.title: Group Presentations and Building the Class Model: The Mkokoteni's Velocity-Time Graph
lessons.observed: What did we observe about the mkokoteni's motion from the table and graph? (For example: velocity rises by 2 m/s every second, giving a straight line through the origin on the v-t graph; distance grows as t², with s = 25 m at 5 s but 100 m at 10 s; the cart hits the lorry at 20 m/s, or 72 km/h.) What did you observe in the group presentations about linear motion in real life?
lessons.learned: What did we learn today? (For example: the gradient of a velocity-time graph is acceleration (2 m/s²); the area under it is displacement (1/2 x 10 x 20 = 100 m); a constant acceleration gives a straight line; the s-t graph is a curve; free fall is the same physics with a = g = 10 m/s²; stopping distance rises sharply with speed.)
lessons.explained: How do we now explain the driving question? (For example: gravity pulls the mkokoteni down the slope all the time, giving a constant acceleration of a = g x 0.2 = 2.0 m/s², so its velocity keeps rising from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s; it starts slowly because it starts from rest and feels sudden because distance grows as t²; the equations of linear motion and the v-t graph let us predict speed and distance at any moment, and they show why higher speeds need much longer stopping distances.)

lessons.title: Consolidation, DQB Review and Final Explanation: Why the Mkokoteni Keeps Getting Faster and How We Predict It
lessons.observed: We observed that the mkokoteni released from rest on the Limuru-Nairobi escarpment slope speeds up steadily: 0 m/s at 0 s, 4 m/s at 2 s, 10 m/s at 5 s and 20 m/s (72 km/h) at 10 s after 100 m. We observed that a mango dropped from a 5 m branch reaches 10 m/s after 1 s, and that objects dropped from 2.0 m took about 0.64 s regardless of what they were.
lessons.learned: We learned that velocity increases by 2 m/s every second because the cart has a constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s² (g x 0.2), caused by gravity pulling it down the slope all the time. We learned the four equations of linear motion, how to choose the right one by listing knowns and the unknown, and that on a velocity-time graph the gradient is the acceleration and the area is the displacement. We learned that free fall is the same motion with a = g = 10 m/s² on a vertical path.
lessons.explained: The mkokoteni keeps getting faster even with no one pushing because gravity acts on it down the slope all the time, giving a constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s². It starts slowly because its velocity begins at 0 m/s, and the crash feels sudden because the distance grows as t² (25 m by 5 s but 100 m by 10 s). Using v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as we can predict that it reaches 20 m/s (72 km/h) after 100 m and 10 s. In a 20 m free fall the same 20 m/s is reached in just 2 s, because the slope gives the cart only 0.2 of g. This is why high speeds need much longer stopping distances and why road-safety rules on steep roads matter.
